records.name: Autophagy
records.tldr: Autophagy delivers cellular material for breakdown and reuse. The amount present, the rate of recycling and whether cells need it to survive are different questions.
records.summary: Macroautophagy encloses cargo in autophagosomes for lysosomal delivery and breakdown. LC3 abundance alone cannot distinguish increased formation from reduced removal. Tandem fluorescent LC3 reporters exploit different responses to acidic and degradative conditions to examine maturation in cell experiments; interpretation requires appropriate controls. Flux and survival dependence need separate tests. In a randomised phase 2 trial of 112 people with advanced pancreatic cancer, adding hydroxychloroquine to gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel did not improve the primary endpoint of survival at 12 months. A drug trial does not by itself establish selective autophagy dependence in a tumour.

Macroautophagy encloses cargo in a double-membrane autophagosome, delivers it through lysosomal fusion and degrades it for reuse. Formation, delivery and breakdown are separate steps; not all lysosomal processes use autophagosomes. Active recycling often supports stress adaptation, whereas autophagy-dependent death requires causal evidence implicating the machinery.

A completed macroautophagosome has separate inner and outer membranes, with space between them. When it fuses with a lysosome, the outer membrane joins the lysosomal boundary, while the inner membrane is degraded before enzymes gain access to the enclosed cargo. Itakura and colleagues located syntaxin 17 on completed autophagosomes, and Tsuboyama and colleagues found that loss of ATG conjugation systems markedly delayed inner-membrane degradation even when fusion occurred. A direct-fusion sketch omits intermediate endosomal interactions described in multicellular organisms; it is not the complete route taken by every compartment.

Product return has evidence in defined systems. In leucine-starved cultured human HEK-293T cells, Wyant and colleagues found that SLC38A9 was needed for leucine made by lysosomal protein breakdown to reach the cytosol; the response also depended on the autophagy protein ATG7. Abu-Remaileh and colleagues measured regulated lysosomal amino-acid exchange in mammalian cells. Yeast experiments identified Atg22, Avt3 and Avt4 as partially redundant vacuolar amino-acid exporters. These results support amino-acid recycling in those systems, without establishing transport of every breakdown product, secretion from the cell or guaranteed growth.

More lipidated LC3-II can reflect greater formation or slower removal. A controlled short lysosomal block and complementary tandem fluorescent LC3 reporter can help examine turnover and delivery to acidic compartments. Equal starting amounts can have different later fates. Little additional accumulation can reflect a late block, low formation or an unsuitable window; it does not establish dependence.

Flux, selected-cargo clearance and survival dependence are different claims. NBR1 experiments identify selective ubiquitinated-cargo handling, not a universal LC3 cargo census. Use time courses, viable-cell normalisation, verified lysosomal inhibition and independent perturbations; autophagy proteins can have other functions. Lower mTOR signalling can change initiation without guaranteeing completed degradation. Typical research outputs include normalised LC3-II band intensity, reporter compartments per cell and selected-cargo disappearance over time. Tested cultures are consumed or perturbed, and prolonged lysosomal inhibition can itself disturb the system. No universal LC3 or flux cutoff selects treatment.

In Karasic and colleagues' randomised phase 2 study of 112 people with advanced pancreatic cancer, adding hydroxychloroquine to gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel increased response rate but did not improve the primary endpoint of survival at 12 months. Response was 38.2% versus 21.1%; 12-month survival was 41% versus 49%. These group results do not show selective autophagy dependence or recommend this combination.

Klionsky's 2021 assay guidelines distinguish LC3 carrier flux from actual cargo or substrate flux. LC3-II is the lipid-attached form of microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3; accumulation can reflect formation or slower removal. Compare treatment alone, a verified lysosomal block such as bafilomycin A1 alone, both together and the relevant baseline, with suitable time and dose windows. An additional LC3-II increase can support turnover under those conditions, but partial inhibition, saturation, low formation or cell death can complicate the comparison. Little change is not a unique diagnosis of an existing late block. A tandem two-colour reporter adds information about acidic delivery, not proof that every cargo completed degradation. Pair markers with an appropriate cargo measurement. Sequestosome 1, SQSTM1/p62, is an adaptor whose abundance also depends on expression and other processes, so one p62 snapshot cannot establish blockage.

A fictional one-hour recycling-station comparison starts with 20 waiting bags in each station. A receives 30 and processes 30, leaving 20; B receives five and processes none, leaving 25. Equal initial piles, including a six-bag schematic snapshot, cannot identify the rate or the later outcome. Bags are not LC3 molecules or assay thresholds: real markers are produced and removed, cargos differ, and a perturbation can affect several steps. Measure completion over time with appropriate controls. Even verified flow does not establish survival dependence; after a specific perturbation, more death can support a protective role, less drug-induced death can support a contribution to that death response, and changed flow with similar survival leaves timing or compensation as possible limits.

Breast-cancer studies illustrate the conditional direction. Bellare 2021 reported that genetic disruption or chloroquine increased talazoparib sensitivity in the tested HR-proficient cells and xenografts. Arun 2015 found that ATG5 reduction partly reduced olaparib-induced apoptosis in BRCA2-mutant HCC-1428 cells, an oestrogen-receptor-positive line rather than a triple-negative model. These different drugs, models and perturbations do not define one protective or death-promoting label for all tumours. Bellare's 2025 correction replaced representative MCF7 images in Figure 5c as well as a liver-histology image in Figure 6f. The authors stated that replicate-based quantification and interpretation were unchanged; that statement is theirs, not an independent validation of the replacement images.

Bulk RNA abundance measures messages across the sampled cell mixture; it does not time cargo flow or establish dependence. ATG13 and the RB1CC1-encoded protein FIP200 participate with ULK1 in initiation machinery, as Ganley 2009 studied, but an alteration in a component does not establish the direction of completed recycling. A mechanistic dependence test should measure the proposed change before extensive death alters the markers, combine complementary readouts, and where feasible perturb more than one autophagy gene at different steps. Klionsky's guidelines also caution that these proteins have other functions. Restoration and independent perturbations strengthen a specific causal explanation without making every genetic manipulation perfectly selective. A lower ATP or metabolic signal alone is neither counted death nor proof of autophagy dependence.

Yamamoto and colleagues found that the cargo receptor NBR1 helped direct MHC-I proteins to lysosomes through an autophagy-dependent route in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma models. This lowered the amount of MHC-I at the cell surface, where it displays antigens to CD8 T cells. In mouse experiments, reducing MHC-I or depleting CD8 T cells reversed tumour control after genetic autophagy inhibition. Chloroquine increased surface MHC-I but, alone, did not significantly reduce tumour weight in the reported experiment; its effects on lysosomes are broad. These model results do not establish that every KRAS-driven cancer depends on autophagy or that blocking it benefits patients.
records.analogy: A recycling station can hold a large pile because more material arrives or because processing has slowed. The pile is an amount; material processed over time is a rate. Neither alone tells you whether the city depends on that station.
interventions: Clinical drug studies and mechanistic dependence tests answer different questions.
Assess flux, selected cargo and survival separately with complementary controls.

records.name: PARP inhibitors
records.tldr: These medicines disrupt DNA repair processes. Some also retain repair proteins on DNA; a repair-gene finding alone does not establish that they will help.
records.summary: PARP inhibitors reduce PARP enzyme activity and can stabilise PARP complexes on damaged DNA. Catalytic output, DNA-associated occupancy, repair capacity and cell survival are different measurements. Experimental sensitivity depends on the current cellular repair state, and repair-restoring changes can contribute to resistance. Clinical eligibility depends on the particular medicine, cancer setting, previous treatment and required companion test; a shared mechanism is not a shared indication.

notes: PARP means poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase, a protein family involved in cellular signalling and repair. PARP1 is one representative. At damaged DNA it can build signals on proteins from chains of the chemical unit ADP-ribose, called poly(ADP-ribose), or PAR. Catalytic inhibition reduces this output. Some inhibitors can also stabilise DNA-associated PARP complexes, often called trapping. A repair-worker analogy separates a reduced call for help from a worker remaining in a doorway; proteins and medicines have no purpose, and the cell has more than one response route.

Murai 2012 compared niraparib, olaparib and veliparib in defined cellular and biochemical systems: niraparib and olaparib trapped PARP-DNA complexes more strongly than veliparib, despite catalytic inhibition being a different comparison. Murai 2014 compared BMN673, now talazoparib, with olaparib and rucaparib. In damaged-DNA cell assays, 0.1 micromolar BMN673 produced a trapping signal comparable to 10 micromolar olaparib, about a 100-fold concentration difference; the purified DNA-binding assay gave a different, roughly 40-fold comparison. Similar catalytic effects did not imply similar trapping. Strongest among compounds tested in 2014 is not a ranking of clinical benefit, tolerated exposure or personal treatment choices.

A DNA-associated protein obstacle can challenge copying without every encounter becoming a measured collision, double-strand break or cell death. Farmer 2005 demonstrated increased sensitivity to PARP inhibition in experimental BRCA-deficient systems. Cong 2021 studied single-stranded replication gaps in cellular models: gap suppression tracked resistance or resensitisation, while restoring fork protection did not always restore resistance in the tested models. Obstacle and gap explanations can coexist, but their relative contribution in a patient's tumour is not established by these experiments. A repair-gene variant alone does not reproduce the functional losses tested in a synthetic-lethal experiment.

Two schematic pictures ask different questions. Matched snapshots of DNA-bound PARP1 with a longer or shorter PAR chain illustrate catalytic output; a generic inhibitor in the catalytic pocket does not measure binding duration. A second picture places approaching copying machinery behind a retained PARP1 complex, with visible separation; it does not show an observed collision, literal backbone conformation or a measured effect size. Reduced catalytic activity and DNA retention can occur together. The arrows therefore lead to further context-dependent measurements, rather than two independent proofs of a clinical mechanism or a drug ranking.

Enzyme assays and PAR immunoassays report catalytic activity or its product. NCI's PAR assay measures PAR levels in specified biospecimens; chromatin-associated PARP measurements instead investigate DNA retention under specified conditions. Repair readouts and survival/regrowth experiments add other information. Murai's experiments used defined cell lines, DNA damage and drug concentrations, so neither a reduced metabolic or ATP signal alone nor a picture establishes irreversible death or its cause. Matched genetic perturbations and appropriate controls are needed to distinguish reduced growth, reduced metabolism and loss of long-term survival.

Waks's selected resistant breast cancer cohort illustrates why historical repair markers and current repair can diverge: four definite or putative BRCA reversion cases acquired RAD51 foci, and other proposed routes included 53BP1 loss and MRE11A amplification. The 53BP1-loss case lacked enough tissue for direct functional confirmation. A historical scar or sequence hypothesis cannot establish a present PARP vulnerability, and this small cohort does not supply an all-patient resistance rule. Biological plausibility, a qualifying label indication and a trial place are separate requirements.

For example, the U.S. olaparib label effective July 2025 specifies adjuvant treatment of adults with deleterious or suspected-deleterious germline BRCA-mutated, HER2-negative high-risk early breast cancer after neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy, selected with an approved companion diagnostic. A tumour-only BRCA result or high scar score cannot replace the germline and disease-setting requirements. That indication does not establish that a different PARP inhibitor, a different setting or a plausible mechanism has the same approval or access conditions.

In a fictional comparison, compounds A and B inhibit PARP catalytic activity similarly, but A retains more PARP on DNA in a culture assay. The conclusion is an assay-specific trapping difference. Useful exposure, survival, safety, resistance and clinical outcomes still need evidence. More trapping in that system does not establish a better treatment, and neither an old scar nor a repair-gene name identifies which effect matters in the current tumour.

Hoslett and colleagues' 2026 preclinical study investigated selective disposal of trapped PARP1 involving TEX264, the protein-remodelling enzyme p97 and LC3-associated lysosomal handling. Autophagic handling of nuclear material is called nucleophagy. Perturbing the machinery increased chromatin-associated PARP1 and PARP-inhibitor sensitivity in the studied systems; complementation and cargo-recognition experiments supported the proposed route. Some trapping experiments also supplied the DNA-damaging agent MMS, so their conditions are not every drug-alone exposure. The authors left the exact export or packaging of nuclear cargo, and macroautophagy versus direct microautophagy, unresolved. A clearance cartoon is therefore a mechanistic model, not established compartment geometry. Expression-survival associations do not validate TEX264 expression as a treatment-response test.

In a fictional culture, more death with a PARP inhibitor plus a lysosomal drug fits several explanations: reduced clearance of trapped PARP, toxicity from the second drug itself, or another altered stress response. Measure chromatin-bound PARP1 over the relevant interval, include both single-drug conditions, and test the proposed clearance machinery with suitable independent perturbation and restoration. Unchanged trapped cargo despite more death argues against that particular clearance explanation. TEX264 or p97 perturbation is complementary evidence, not automatically perfectly selective, because proteins can have other functions. Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine alter lysosomal processes broadly. Survival alone, high recycling RNA or a broad lysosomal effect does not identify selective trapped-PARP disposal or establish patient benefit.
records.principle: Catalytic inhibition reduces PAR signalling; some inhibitors also stabilise DNA-associated PARP complexes. Protein obstacles and replication gaps are studied mechanisms, with effects dependent on repair state, exposure and the experimental or clinical setting.
strengths: Oral medicines with defined, setting-specific approved uses
Catalytic and DNA-retention effects can be studied separately
limitations: Blood-cell toxicity and other harms depend on product and exposure
Repair-restoring changes can contribute to resistance
Laboratory trapping potency does not rank clinical benefit

records.name: PI3K / AKT / mTOR
records.tldr: This network links growth signals and nutrients to protein production, metabolism and recycling. Different branches can respond differently to an intervention.
records.summary:
Class I PI3K phosphorylates a membrane lipid, producing PIP3; PTEN removes its position-3 phosphate. AKT and mTOR are protein kinases. A PIP3 lipid result and an AKT1 Ser473 phosphosite result are therefore different molecular measurements. Document specimen preservation, cell mixture, protein site, timing, exposure, comparator and total-protein normalization before interpreting a change as activity or dependence.

Membrane recruitment helps organize AKT activation. PDK1 phosphorylates AKT1 Thr308, whereas the rictor-mTOR complex supplies Ser473 phosphorylation in the defined experimental route. AKT can inhibit TSC2, relieving the TSC1/2 brake on RHEB, which promotes mTORC1 signaling. The diagram's indirect AKT-to-mTORC1 connection stands for these regulatory steps; it is not direct phosphorylation of mTORC1 by AKT.

Raptor-containing mTORC1 and rictor-containing mTORC2 are distinct complexes. mTORC1 regulates protein production and autophagy-initiation machinery; releasing initiation restraint is not proof of completed recycling flux. Harrington linked S6K activity to reduced IRS-1 function, and O'Reilly observed increased IRS-1 and AKT signaling after RAD001 in cell models and treated tumors. Feedback release can change an output without proving that a combination improves outcomes in every setting.

In a fictional mTORC1 perturbation, lower production-regulator phosphorylation followed by higher AKT1 Ser473 and unchanged growth supports biochemical changes, not essentiality or failed engagement; timing alone does not prove the feedback connection. Test the proposed wiring and functional outcome independently. The FDA's 2023 capivasertib-with-fulvestrant approval specified adults with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, qualifying PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN alterations on an approved test and specified prior endocrine treatment or early recurrence. It is not a TNBC indication inferred from a pathway label.

notes: PI3K means phosphoinositide 3-kinase; AKT is also called protein kinase B. Mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1, mTORC1, integrates growth and nutrient inputs. PTEN, phosphatase and tensin homolog, removes a phosphate from a PI3K-generated lipid signal. These protein and lipid reactions need their own readouts. Ibrahim 2012 found that PI3K inhibition reduced BRCA1/2 expression and increased PARP-inhibitor sensitivity in the BRCA-proficient triple-negative breast cancer models studied. A second branch concerns mTORC1 restraint of ULK1-associated autophagy initiation, studied by Kim 2011. Releasing an initiation brake does not establish completed cargo degradation or protective recycling. The two branches can change together without revealing the net survival effect. A model already lacking the relevant repair function cannot be assumed to gain the same vulnerability as one in which that function is newly reduced; measure protein and repair function, flux and survival under the actual compound, dose and schedule.

Rapalogs, PI3K or AKT inhibitors and ATP-site mTOR kinase inhibitors are different interventions. In Rodrik-Outmezguine's 2011 models, inhibiting both mTOR complexes initially reduced AKT Ser473 and Thr308 phosphorylation, but relief of receptor feedback later restored Thr308 phosphorylation and AKT signalling while Ser473 remained suppressed. A Ser473 result therefore did not measure all AKT activity. O'Reilly's rapalog study and Harrington's IRS feedback work likewise explain why lower mTORC1 output can coexist with increased upstream signalling. These are measured responses in specified systems, not inevitable behaviour or a universal combination prescription.

In a fictional experiment, repair RNA falls, an mTORC1-associated phosphosite falls, AKT phosphorylation rises and more autophagosomes appear. The RNA concerns messages; confirm the proposed protein and repair consequence. A validated site change concerns that output at that time, while the AKT change may fit feedback without proving every downstream effect. Autophagosome amount does not establish completed flux, and no survival conclusion has yet been supplied. Growth and energy inputs also differ: Gwinn 2008 linked AMPK phosphorylation of raptor to mTORC1 restraint during energy stress. Slower costly building work and better survival can coexist. Named S6, 4E-BP1, AKT and AMPK-target sites need their own controls, total-protein context and timing; bulk RNA is not a kinase-activity meter.

PIK3CA encodes the PI3K-alpha catalytic subunit. PIKFYVE is a different lipid kinase involved in endolysosomal regulation. Similar names do not make them the same target, and evidence about one does not automatically describe the other.
records.analogy: Think of a factory: the receptor is the order desk, PI3K and AKT are the managers relaying the order, PTEN is the accountant cancelling orders, and mTOR is the assembly line. Cancer forges orders (PIK3CA mutation) or fires the accountant (PTEN loss).

records.name: Controlled perturbation experiment
records.tldr: Controlled perturbations deliberately change specified factors and compare responses with suitable controls. A model response alone does not prove its mechanism or patient benefit.
records.summary: A controlled perturbation deliberately changes a defined factor and measures the response against appropriate comparison conditions. Vehicle, positive, negative and mechanism controls answer different questions. A reproducible response can support an experimental claim without establishing its proposed mechanism or patient benefit. Baseline growth, timing, dose and the actual unit assigned to treatment matter.

notes: A vehicle control contains the carrier without the active treatment; an untreated condition asks a different question if the carrier has effects. A positive control checks that the assay can detect a known relevant response, while a negative or non-targeting control estimates background under its design. Another independent way to disrupt the same function can support a mechanism, and a rescue restores a function to test whether that reverses the response here. Off-target effects, incomplete restoration and model context limit interpretation. These are questions for matched model, timing and readout; no one control proves specificity or patient benefit, and agreement between similar readouts is not automatically independent mechanistic confirmation.

Keep what changed, the comparator, concentration or dose range, timing, assignment, readout and units, sample identities, replicate structure and variability. Repeated wells address variation under their preparation and allocation; independently obtained biological samples address another source of variation. Many wells from one tumour do not become independent patients, and repetition or a small p-value does not repair a missing comparison. A two-drug experiment needs vehicle, both single drugs and the combination. A larger combination effect than either single drug is not automatically synergy; that claim needs a stated reference model.

Fictional direct counts: vehicle-treated cells increase from 100 to 200 while drug-treated cells remain at 100. The endpoint drug count is half the vehicle count without measured net decline from the starting count, so calling it 50 per cent killing overstates the observation. Slower growth, death and a molecular change require their own readouts; direct death or recovery measurements could address further questions. Hafner and colleagues showed that conventional IC50 and maximal-effect measures depend on cell divisions during an assay and developed growth-rate metrics to address that dependence. A real experimental response does not by itself establish the responsible target or clinical benefit.

A fictional two-drug table normalises remaining viability to vehicle at 100 per cent: A leaves 70, B leaves 80, and combination examples leave 56 or 30. Highest single agent uses the better single-drug effect, a 70 per cent remaining-viability reference here. Bliss independence predicts 0.70 times 0.80 = 0.56, or 56 per cent. Both combinations exceed the HSA effect; 56 matches Bliss while 30 exceeds it at that dose pair. A further combination leaving 65 exceeds HSA but not Bliss. Loewe additivity instead needs equivalent-dose information from suitable individual dose-response curves; this one-point table cannot establish it. Report the model, dose-pair pattern, uncertainty and schedule. Interaction relative to a reference does not identify a biological mechanism, tolerable human exposure or a treatment choice.

A rescue restores a proposed missing function or supply and tests whether a defined effect reverses. Adding a cake mix back after its removal implicates the mixture without identifying flour, sugar or another ingredient; likewise, broad mevalonate add-back does not isolate cholesterol. More specific branch perturbations and appropriate add-backs can narrow the explanation. Partial rescue can reflect incomplete delivery or restoration as well as additional contributors, so it does not prove a second cause. Place the add-back relative to the blocked step: supplying GGPP after an upstream synthesis block is different from inhibiting the transferase that uses GGPP, which the added substrate cannot simply be assumed to bypass. Include restoration-only and matched controls, verify the restored process and distinguish growth, morphology and death. A genetic perturbation also has its own specificity limits.

Attribute each readout to the relevant cells. An ATP-based signal can change through cell number or per-cell metabolism, and slower single-cell mass accumulation does not by itself show death. Direct death measurements and regrowth after washout ask further questions; regrowth concerns surviving cells, not revival of cells already dead. A mixed culture can change composition, and a nonmalignant-cell label alone does not establish a validated healthy-tissue control. Ladan's breast-slice chemotherapy assay was compared with response during preoperative treatment in a defined setting. That assay-specific validation does not validate every postoperative combination, human exposure or clinical decision. An inadequate viable preparation should remain uninterpretable rather than be called resistant.

records.name: Functional (ex vivo) drug testing
records.tldr: Functional drug testing measures a defined response to medicines in collected living material under laboratory conditions.
records.summary: Functional drug testing exposes a defined living preparation to medicines and measures a specified response. Preparations may use dissociated cells, expanded organoids or short-term tissue cultures. Feasibility, outcome agreement and benefit from using a result to choose care are separate questions and must be tied to the actual assay version, cancer, treatment and setting.

Input suitability and recovery must be demonstrated for the method. Testing and endpoint processing use finite material. Output needs units, denominator, normalisation and uncertainty; acceptance criteria must be defined for the actual method. Handling evidence is method-specific. Ladan and colleagues collected breast tissue in their specified medium, cut 300 micrometre slices and assessed morphology, proliferation and apoptosis after three-day exposure. This is not a general transport or storage protocol for all screens. Growth-rate methods show why baseline counts and control division affect interpretation. Retain failures and exclusions; failed preparation is not clinical resistance. Mechanism-relevant controls test whether the claimed interaction can occur; absent required cells or unrealistic exposures can make an experiment uninformative even when a numerical response is available. A laboratory concentration is not a safe human dose.

Fictional example. A well has half the metabolic signal but the same identified viable tumour-cell endpoint count as control. This establishes a changed proxy, not half the cells killed; endpoint equality also does not reconstruct every division and death. Separate death, target engagement, safe human dosing and clinical benefit remain questions. This is an arithmetic and interpretation exercise, not observed patient data. Possible readouts include cell number, metabolism, mass, growth and death. Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is a cellular energy molecule measured by some luminescence assays. Promega's primary assay guidance states that cellular ATP content varies with cell type and physiology and can alter the relation between cell number and light output. A lower ATP signal can therefore reflect fewer cells or a per-cell change, rather than a counted death fraction. Source: https://www.promega.com/-/media/files/resources/protocols/technical-bulletins/0/celltiter-glo-luminescent-cell-viability-assay-protocol.pdf

Restivo and colleagues generated organoids from matched fresh and slow-frozen colorectal tumour tissue from two patients with stage IV disease. Their specified slow-freezing protocol used a cryoprotectant to preserve living material, and the frozen-derived cultures took longer to form than the fresh-derived cultures. This is evidence of recovery under that protocol, not equivalence of all fresh, snap-frozen and viable-cryopreserved samples or a guaranteed turnaround. The handling history, recovery, malignant identity and assay quality need checking for the intended experiment. Preserved molecular material alone does not establish a recoverable living model. Source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-022-04025-0

Read a model study as a sequence of explicitly defined groups: people or specimens offered or submitted, preparations yielding a usable model, results compared with a clinical outcome, and results agreeing under the stated rule. Eligibility exclusions, absent tumour, laboratory failures, missing outcomes and people not receiving the treatment belong to different steps. State whether the unit is a person, specimen or treatment comparison; one person can contribute more than one. A percentage among compared cases cannot describe everyone originally offered testing, and an analysis exclusion is not automatically a failed culture. Keep the drug, cancer, treatment history, outcome, clock and assay version attached rather than ranking different studies as competing accuracy scores.

The prospective single-arm SENSOR study enrolled 61 people with metastatic colorectal cancer: 54 were eligible, 31 organoids were generated, 25 cultures were screened against eight drugs and nineteen showed a substantial laboratory response. Six people received an organoid-selected treatment, three vistusertib and three capivasertib, with no objective clinical responses. That observation concerns this panel and selected population; it neither establishes benefit from using the assay nor proves that every organoid method is ineffective. Guillen and colleagues' breast-model report describes a complete response in one person with metastatic triple-negative disease after a model-nominated treatment. That case demonstrates feasibility, without a comparison estimating how often the strategy helps.

Randomised outcome evidence must be assessed for the named assay and use rather than declared absent for all functional testing in solid tumours. Ranjan and colleagues reported a 2023 trial of ChemoID selection versus physician choice from the same chemotherapy list in 78 people with recurrent glioblastoma under the 2016 WHO definition. Enrolment stopped after a prespecified efficacy analysis; the intention-to-treat report gave median overall survival of twelve versus 7.5 months. Participants could provide viable tumour through surgery or biopsy, so the findings do not include every patient with recurrent glioblastoma. Cordgenics supported the assay resources, and two authors declared licensed intellectual-property interests. This is evidence for the studied strategy and population, without validating another assay, organoid system, postoperative breast decision or universal treatment rule.

Consider an entirely invented tumour-only organoid experiment from one donor and one characterised preparation, with three wells per condition. Drug A is tested at 0.1, 0.3 and 1 micromoles per litre for 48 hours with matched carrier and handling. The planned primary readout is calibrated viable tumour-cell count at the start and endpoint, with cell identity checked. Vehicle, a positive control with an expected response and a target perturbation or rescue ask different questions. Their actual results must be documented; the illustrative counts do not show that every control passed. Three wells are not three donors. This preparation supplies neither immune cells, full human metabolism nor a healthy-organ toxicity measurement, and these example exposures are not human doses.

In that fictional experiment, both groups start at 1,000 viable tumour cells per well. At 48 hours and the middle exposure of 0.3 micromoles per litre, the median across three wells is 2,000 for vehicle and 1,000 for treatment. Treatment is at 50 percent of the later vehicle count and 100 percent of its own starting count. That establishes no net increase, not 50 percent killing or absence of division. Reduced division or division balanced by death can give that endpoint; time-course and suitable division/death measurements distinguish explanations. Keep each well and its variation rather than treating the median as three independent patients.

Two matched parallel aliquots add different fictional readouts to the same comparison; they do not track the original cells individually. Mean buoyant mass is 20 picograms per measured cell at the start, 21 with vehicle and 16 with treatment, so the treated mean is 80 percent of its starting value. Metabolic signal is 100 arbitrary units at the start, 190 with vehicle and 70 with treatment: 70 divided by 190 is about 36.8 percent, a 63.2 percent reduction relative to vehicle. Neither is a killed-cell fraction. A changing population mean is not an individual-cell trajectory, and buoyant mass depends on cell volume and the difference between cell and fluid density. It is not dry mass, a count of living cells or a measurement of a particular death mechanism.

records.name: Double-strand break repair: HR versus end joining
records.tldr: Cells can repair breaks through both DNA strands using a matching template or several end-joining routes. The available template, cell state and broken ends affect which route can operate.
records.summary:
Double-strand breaks can be repaired through matching-template homologous recombination or several end-joining routes. Homologous repair often uses the sister chromatid after DNA copying. The substrate, available template and cell-cycle state affect which route can operate.

Preparing a double-strand break for homologous repair includes DNA end resection in the 5′ to 3′ direction, leaving protruding 3′ single-stranded ends. RAD51 helps a prepared strand find and pair with a complementary strand in matching duplex DNA, displacing the other template strand into a D-loop. DNA synthesis can then extend the invading end using the template. Synthesis-dependent strand annealing can finish as a noncrossover repair: the extended strand leaves the template and pairs with the other broken end. Other homologous-repair routes can have crossover outcomes, so using an intact template does not mean every repair leaves donor and recipient arrangements unchanged. Purified bacterial RecA structures reveal strand-pairing intermediates; they are not direct measurements of human RAD51 repair in a tumour.

Classical nonhomologous end joining reconnects ends without requiring a long matching template and can preserve compatible ends. Microhomology-associated joining uses short matching sequences after end processing. Theta-mediated end joining names a POLQ-mediated mechanism; finding short matches alone does not identify that enzyme. These routes overlap in outcomes without becoming interchangeable definitions.

Ku binds broken ends, and ligase IV with supporting factors can help align and seal them; difficult ends can require processing. Resection exposes single-stranded regions for alternative joining, where short matches can align and intervening sequence can be lost. Purified-factor experiments, defined chromosome-break reporters and controlled cellular studies test particular substrates and factor dependencies, not a universal menu for every break.

A fictional top-strand sequence CA-GAC-TT|AA-GAC-GT has 14 base pairs before joining. A selected short-match product CA-GAC-GT retains seven, losing the four-base TTAA interval and one three-base GAC repeat. For a selected alignment of GAC with its complementary CTG sequence, trimming the unmatched TT flaps leaves seven paired positions and two backbone nicks to seal, without a gap to fill. Other substrates can require synthesis; this arithmetic and schematic geometry are not measured repair frequencies.

Sequence a repaired junction and measure a defined repair reporter, then perturb the proposed factor with specificity controls and, where feasible, rescue. Repair fraction, junction distribution and cell survival are distinct outputs. A deletion with microhomology is compatible with a joining route, but does not demonstrate POLQ dependence, selective killing or benefit from a POLQ inhibitor in a patient. Viable-cell and purified-component studies have model-specific input and material costs.

records.name: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA)
records.tldr: Cell-free DNA is DNA outside intact cells in a collected sample. Tumour-derived DNA is one possible part of that mixture; its amount depends on the specimen and method.
records.summary:
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is DNA outside intact cells in a specimen. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is the tumour-derived part of the plasma DNA mixture, rather than a different material competing with cfDNA. DNA from non-tumour tissues can contribute much of that mixture, as illustrated by Moss and colleagues' methylation-atlas study. Total extracted DNA is therefore not a tumour measurement. A finite evaluated aliquot can contain no qualifying tumour signal even when disease exists elsewhere.

Liquid biopsy describes a specimen approach. A test may track known tumour features, look for predefined mutation, methylation or fragment patterns, or profile detectable alterations. Its target coverage, origin checks, sample requirements and calling rule determine the claim. Genotyping, residual-disease monitoring and screening have different intended uses; a method label does not validate every use or locate the source of a plasma signal.

notes: Source classes: cfDNA is DNA outside intact cells in a sample, and ctDNA is the tumour-derived part of that pool, so the two are related materials and not rival tests. In healthy donors a methylation atlas of 25 tissues and cell types attributed plasma cfDNA to white blood cells (55%), erythrocyte progenitors (30%), vascular endothelial cells (10%) and hepatocytes (1%) (Moss 2018). A tumour adds DNA only when it contributes, and the tumour share may be small or absent in the sample drawn even when cancer exists elsewhere.

Scale: plasma DNA fragments show a pattern reminiscent of nuclease-cleaved nucleosomes with a peak at 166 base pairs (Lo 2010, in maternal plasma), and tumour-derived fragments are enriched at 90 to 150 base pairs (Mouliere 2018). One assay input in a breast-cancer comparison was 4,500 amplifiable copies, about 15 nanograms (Santonja 2023), and at about 3.3 picograms per haploid genome copy 1 nanogram is roughly 300 copies (arithmetic from genome size). In a fictional single-locus model with 4,500 amplifiable opportunities and target-allele probability 1 in 100,000, the expected target count is 0.045. The target-allele probability is not automatically a tumour-DNA fraction: copy number, variant multiplicity and clone representation matter.

Yield is not origin: in a fictional experiment equal 1 mL plasma aliquots give 2 and 4 nanograms of cfDNA and no tumour-attributed signal is reported. Total DNA doubled, but tumour fraction and any tumour-DNA fold change cannot be calculated because tumour attribution was not measured. A fragment's source needs evidence such as paired white-blood-cell and tumour sequencing (Razavi 2019), and a variant seen in plasma is not automatically tumour-derived.

Method card: measures selected features of plasma DNA by a stated sequencing or molecular method, from a finite plasma aliquot that testing consumes. Output is detected or not detected, variant fractions, molecule concentrations or model estimates, each with its own unit. It cannot give an all-body cell count, lesion location, viability or treatment benefit, and validity belongs to the exact specimen, assay version and intended use.

Collection conditions can change the mixture before testing: blood-cell breakdown adds genomic DNA and can dilute a tumour fraction. The NCI biospecimen practices document, revised February 2025, prefers plasma to serum. Its protocol recommends EDTA, accepts acid citrate dextrose, and advises avoiding heparin and citrate; the literature-summary section separately reports results with several anticoagulants when processing was immediate. For EDTA blood the protocol prefers centrifugation within 2 hours and accepts up to 4 hours at room temperature or 24 hours at 4 degrees Celsius; it recommends stabilising tubes for anticipated delays over 2 hours. These are recommendations for that specimen workflow, not a universal acceptance rule for every assay. Extraction and library preparation then retain only some available molecules, so the volume drawn is not the volume evaluated.

Reading an assay report starts with the specimen and collection date, the plasma volume actually evaluated, DNA quality and recovery, origin checks, and the rule that turns a signal into a call. Low shedding, damaged input or failed quality controls can limit interpretation; a failed assay is a separate result from no qualifying signal. Genotyping, response monitoring and residual-disease detection are different intended uses. In its November 2024 drug-development guidance, FDA asks for validation of the complete workflow, representative clinical samples, the input range and prespecified calling cut-offs; validation of one use does not establish another.

A useful result ledger keeps six questions together: when the sample was collected and where that date sits relative to treatment or surgery; the assay and version; the specimen, evaluated input and quality qualifications; the reported state, including detected, not detected, indeterminate or failed; the quantity, unit and numerical qualifications; and the applicable detection and quantitation criteria. Keep the report-release date separately. Two reports arriving together may describe different biological moments, and an invalid sample or failed reference build is not a negative plasma result.

In a fictional comparison, one assay reports not detected and another reports a low detected signal. That alone does not identify an erroneous test. Compare the actual samples and collection dates, targets, input, controls and calling criteria before interpreting the disagreement. A valid negative says that the evaluated sample did not meet that method's qualifying-signal rule. It cannot distinguish every possibility: there may be no residual tumour signal, too few relevant fragments may have reached the aliquot, or the tracked features may not represent the remaining cells. This reading exercise sets no repeat-draw schedule.

records.name: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA)
records.tldr: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) consists of fragments of DNA shed by tumour cells into the blood, detectable with sensitive sequencing.
records.summary: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is made up of DNA fragments shed by tumour cells into the bloodstream, where they form only a small fraction of all cell-free DNA and are detected with sensitive sequencing. Its uses span genotyping for companion diagnostics, tracking resistance mutations such as EGFR T790M and ESR1, molecular residual disease, early detection and response monitoring. Shedding varies with tumour type and burden, and clonal haematopoiesis can confound results. The term underpins the Liquid biopsy (ctDNA), MRD / molecular residual disease testing and Multi-cancer early detection (MCED) technologies, and it appears in the SERENA-6, CIRCULATE-Japan and IMvigor011 trials and in ideas on molecular-progression switching beyond ESR1 and HPV ctDNA to guide cervical cancer therapy.

notes: Detection depends on stage and tumour type: with digital PCR-based methods in 640 patients, ctDNA was found in more than 75% of people with advanced pancreatic, ovarian, colorectal, bladder, gastro-oesophageal, breast, melanoma, hepatocellular and head and neck cancers, and in fewer than 50% of primary brain, renal, prostate or thyroid cancers. In localised disease it was found in 73% of colorectal, 57% of gastro-oesophageal, 48% of pancreatic and 50% of breast adenocarcinomas, and it was often present in people with no detectable circulating tumour cells (Bettegowda 2014). The assay, specimen and population are part of each figure.

ctDNA is a subset of cell-free DNA, and not every plasma variant is tumour-derived: in paired plasma and white-blood-cell sequencing, 53.2% of cfDNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 people without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis (Razavi 2019). A ctDNA result is also a quantity with a unit (molecules per millilitre, a fraction, or a call), and the same number means different things under each.

Lung cancer: plasma genotyping at diagnosis is non-inferior to tissue for finding a guideline biomarker (27.3% against 21.3% in 282 patients), has 100% positive predictive value for the alterations with approved drugs, returns in 9 days against 15, and raises detection by 48% when added to tissue (Leighl 2019). Clinical sensitivity against tissue is 80%, so a negative plasma result rules nothing out and the guideline permits plasma to rule in only (Lindeman 2018). Serial plasma after starting treatment also separates the patients whose resistant clone was already present, within three weeks (Oxnard 2018).

records.name: ctDNA and imaging discordance
records.tldr: A blood DNA result and an imaging result can seem to disagree because they sample different material, regions, times and signals. A mismatch is a question to resolve, not a verdict on either test.
records.summary:
A circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) assay looks for tumour-associated features in a finite sample of cell-free DNA. How much tumour DNA reaches the sampled blood varies between lesions, and recovery, background DNA, the features tracked and the assay's detection limit all shape the call. Imaging measures a defined region through a physical signal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast can report contrast enhancement or the volume of enhancing tissue, which is not a direct count of viable cancer cells. The two tests can therefore differ without either being wrong, and neither automatically replaces the other.

They can also share information. In Magbanua and colleagues' pilot of 84 women having neoadjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer, ctDNA concentration was correlated with MRI functional tumour volume at all four time points, with Spearman correlations of 0.42 to 0.49, and patients with detectable ctDNA had a higher median volume. Agreement was partial, and adding ctDNA early in treatment to volume-based prediction of pathological complete response gave only a numerical gain that was not statistically significant. ctDNA positivity after treatment added significantly to volume for predicting distant recurrence and death. A mismatch calls for checking dates, assay limits, the imaged region and the exact finding. It does not by itself show a false test or hidden metastatic disease.

notes: Method card, what is compared: a sampled molecular signal in plasma and a regional physical signal from a named imaging protocol. Their units, dates and thresholds stay separate, and the comparison is only as good as the date alignment of the two acquisitions.

Table, blood side: input is a blood draw and the plasma and recovered DNA analysed, and testing consumes an aliquot. Output is a qualifying call plus a defined concentration or fraction, read with the assay's detection and quantitation rules. Failure modes are low shedding, finite input, poor recovery and background or blood-cell variants.

Table, imaging side: input is the imaged region and a protocol, and contrast or tracer use depends on the modality. Output is size, volume, uptake or a qualitative finding read against protocol-specific response criteria. Failure modes are artefacts, non-tumour contributions to the signal and technique that differs between visits.

Table, what each cannot tell: blood alone cannot locate a lesion or give a cell count. Imaging alone cannot count viable tumour cells, and enhancement can have more than one tissue cause. Neither agreement nor disagreement shows that a treatment change would help, which is a clinical-utility question.

Evidence read: Magbanua's pilot (84 patients, MTM/mL against MRI functional tumour volume) found correlation at T0 to T3 with rho 0.49, 0.42, 0.42 and 0.43, and its authors call the findings preliminary in a limited cohort needing larger validation. It supports partial agreement and does not set a rule for redirecting treatment.

Interpretation rule, from finite sampling: a plasma aliquot can hold no tumour molecule when the true share is small, so no qualifying ctDNA signal alongside an abnormal MRI region does not show the region is only scar. The converse holds too: a clear image does not exclude tumour DNA in blood. Each result answers only its own question.

Source attribution comes first: a positive plasma variant may come from a blood-cell clone rather than a tumour. In Razavi's paired sequencing, 53.2% of cell-free DNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 people without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis, so a discordant positive needs origin checks before it is read as occult disease.

Half-life, scoped: Diehl and colleagues estimated a ctDNA half-life after surgery of 114 minutes by evaluating one subject whose plasma was sampled at several early times after complete resection in a study of 162 plasma samples from 18 subjects with colorectal cancer (Diehl 2008). That is a single-subject estimate of post-resection clearance in colorectal cancer, not a universal cfDNA half-life, a breast-cancer figure or a blood-draw schedule. DNA release and clearance can change sooner than visible tissue structure, which is a reason to align the dates of the blood and imaging acquisitions.

Use the blood collection date and imaging acquisition date to compare biology, then keep the reporting dates as a separate measure of when the information became available. Imaging does not remove a tissue aliquot for molecular analysis; contrast or tracer use belongs to the specific protocol. Agreement can reflect shared dependence on disease burden and is not two independent proofs of the same mechanism. Combining measurements into a decision rule needs validation of the combination and its intended outcome.

In a fictional early-breast-cancer example, a negative plasma result is not an examination of the breast tumour bed or regional nodes. It cannot by itself establish pathological complete response or validate skipping surgery. Using a result to remove a treatment needs evidence for that decision strategy and its clinical outcomes, beyond showing that an assay can detect a signal. This is an interpretation limit, not a claim that no omission study exists.

The two-window comparison is about scope. A finite plasma aliquot contains extracellular DNA, of which tumour-derived fragments may be one part; breast MRI observes regional, sequence-dependent features rather than individual cancer cells. Contrast enhancement reflects vascular and contrast-delivery behaviour as well as the acquisition protocol; it is not a one-to-one viable-cell count. In the 84-person I-SPY2 MRI pilot, functional tumour volume summed voxels meeting 70% enhancement about two and a half minutes after contrast, inside a manually drawn box around the lesion. A camera-and-stream analogy illustrates those two sampled views without promising that every tumour sheds DNA. Keep the imaging method visible: mammography uses X-rays, ultrasound uses sound, and PET/CT combines tracer-distribution images with anatomical CT images. A formal response category needs its framework, comparison timepoint and findings outside a selected lesion measurement. None of these measurements is an interchangeable all-body tumour-cell number.

Four patterns illustrate the reading boundary. A smaller lesion and lower detected blood signal mean that both recorded measures fell in their own units, not that pCR or eradication of distant disease is proved. A residual scan finding with undetected blood leaves viability, treatment effects and other causes unresolved. Detected blood with no suspicious finding in the scanned region does not establish the signal's location, full extent or best intervention. If neither shows qualifying evidence, neither has proved zero microscopic disease or justified omitting indicated treatment. These are interpretation examples, not an action algorithm; disagreement alone does not establish pseudoprogression.

In a fictional course, a breast lesion becomes less enhancing, blood changes from detected to not detected, and surgery later finds residual invasive cancer. There is no contradiction: imaging features, a finite molecular sample and removed tissue answer different questions. Only the specified tissue assessment establishes the residual disease in this example. A smaller scan finding and undetected blood can therefore be favourable observations without confirming pCR. Conversely, a later positive blood result with clear regional breast imaging calls for review of sample qualification, origin, dates and clinical context; it is not itself a diagnosis of distant metastasis.

Magbanua and colleagues' 2025 analysis evaluated 723 high-risk I-SPY2 patients across hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, triple-negative and HER2-positive subtypes. Combining ctDNA with residual cancer burden refined prognostic groups, but analyses within those groups used smaller subsets, some too small for multivariable adjustment. The authors also found retained patient-specific assay variants in sampled resistant tumours from patients whose post-treatment plasma was negative. These results support studying risk information and shedding; they do not turn negative presurgical blood into tissue pCR or demonstrate that a blood-guided omission strategy improves outcomes.

Adding receptor measurements introduces another question to a blood and imaging comparison. A sequenced clonotype's sampled abundance does not directly measure its antigen, effector activity or total cell count. Even a controlled secretion or killing result belongs to its tested stimulus and targets. Collecting the measurements together does not link a particular receptor to the tumour DNA signal. Retain time, compartment, chain definition, abundance unit, controls and independent target-recognition evidence; combining the results does not make a validated treatment rule.

In a fictional comparison using compatible measurements, tumour DNA is stable or rising in two patterns and falls in two others, while a receptor measure changes little or increases. Stable or rising DNA with little repertoire change raises questions about the tumour, immunity and assay adequacy without diagnosing resistance or mandating a tissue or spatial test. With greater repertoire change it still does not prove a physical barrier or an antigen-specific response that failed. Falling DNA with little repertoire change does not assign the effect to chemotherapy or show that useful immunity is absent. Falling DNA with greater repertoire change does not prove that immune learning caused control. These are sampled observations, not validated best-response categories, proof of clinical benefit or instructions to change treatment.

records.name: Protein
records.tldr: Proteins are amino-acid products that provide structure, catalysis, transport and signaling. A detected fragment and a complete working protein are different findings.
records.summary: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

records.name: RNA
records.tldr: RNA is a family of molecules with several jobs. Messenger RNA provides a protein-making template; other RNAs help build, regulate or carry out cellular processes.
records.summary: RNA, short for ribonucleic acid, uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.

records.name: Gene
records.tldr: A gene is a DNA region that produces a functional RNA message. Some messages encode proteins; others work as RNA.
records.summary: A protein-coding gene supplies RNA that can be translated into a polypeptide, while a noncoding RNA gene produces a functional RNA. Promoters and other regulatory regions influence transcription in a cell-dependent context. One gene can have several transcript versions. Exons are retained regions of a specified processed transcript and can include untranslated sequence; introns are removed by splicing. Coding sequence is the translated part of a coding message. A gene name alone does not specify a transcript, coding interval or protein product.

records.name: Central dogma and molecular information flow
records.tldr: DNA copying, making RNA and making a protein are different processes. Following the route helps identify what each molecular test actually measured.
records.summary: Replication makes DNA from DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. Translation reads the coding sequence of a message in three-base codons to build a polypeptide; the transcript and reading frame matter. Functional noncoding RNAs do not need to become protein. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant viral and retrotransposon contexts. This information-flow map is not a guarantee that every DNA change produces a measured RNA or protein change.

DNA presence, RNA abundance, intact protein, location and activity require their own evidence. Neither a gene-level RNA count nor a sequence prediction establishes a fixed protein amount or clinical effect.

For a nuclear protein-coding gene in a eukaryotic cell, transcription occurs in the nucleus and the message reaches cytoplasmic ribosomes for translation. A delivered messenger RNA can begin at cytoplasmic translation without requiring genomic integration. This does not imply an empty nucleus or removal of existing nuclear DNA. Neither DNA nor an untranslated message is itself the finished receptor protein. Translation alone does not establish correct folding, processing, transport or function at the cell surface.

In the recipe analogy, the DNA template is retained while an RNA copy is assembled. Translation uses a message as instructions for joining amino acids; the RNA molecule is not the material converted into the protein. The arrows name these processes rather than showing that a reported DNA change produced a measured message or working product. Noncoding RNA lies outside this simplified protein-coding route. Questions about production, location and activity remain open until suitable evidence addresses them.

records.name: Bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and the full transcriptome
records.tldr: Bulk RNA sequencing measures captured messages pooled across a tissue sample, including contributions from multiple cell types.
records.summary: RNA carries cellular messages; bulk sequencing samples those messages from combined tissue after protocol-specific capture and preparation. Analysis assigns usable observations to genes or transcripts and applies a defined comparison scale. A change can reflect cell composition, expression within cells or both. Gene totals can conceal transcript differences, and pooled RNA does not directly establish protein localisation, pathway flux or drug dependence.

Bulk RNA-seq extracts RNA, prepares a library (often cDNA), may select mRNA or deplete rRNA or capture regions; bulk does not mean equal capture of all molecules.
Reads or fragments are assigned to genes or transcripts; shared sequences make assignment ambiguous; a count table is already shaped by preparation and analysis.
A bulk signal can rise because more cells of a type contribute, expression within them rises, or both; deconvolution estimates contributions under a model and does not separate cells.
Gene-level counts can hide isoform differences; a mutant or splice product needs sequence or junction evidence.

Bulk RNA can nominate expressed targets and summarise programmes but does not establish cell origin, surface protein, pathway flux or drug dependence; zero reads is not absence; thousands of genes from one biopsy are not thousands of patients.

Fictional teaching exercise: With equal RNA per cell, a lymphocyte-only marker and 100-cell pieces, raising lymphocytes from 20 to 40 doubles the pooled marker (20 to 40 stipulated molecules) without changing any cancer cell.
Record sampled region and RNA integrity; research profiling differs from a validated clinical RNA test.

Record protocol-compatible preservation, sampled region, RNA integrity and material consumed by extraction. Track capture, sequence assignment, read/fragment units, normalisation and transcript calls. Preparation time varies; reference material, process controls and biological replicates test different uncertainties. Degradation, contamination, ambiguous annotation, batch and mixture shifts constrain purpose-specific cutoffs and clinical intended-use validation.

A larger raw count can be a smaller share of a library. In an invented example, ten captured counts out of 10,000 give 1,000 counts per million, while twenty out of 100,000 give 200. Keep the counted unit and library-size definition. Counts per million scale by that denominator; transcripts per million also use transcript-length information under the chosen quantification method. These relative scales are not interchangeable, do not recover the total RNA made per cell and are not protein counts. A base-two log fold change of plus one corresponds to a ratio of two, and plus two to four under the stated normalization. A reference near zero can make a ratio large while the underlying signal remains small; these are mathematical examples, not biological cutoffs.

Check library chemistry before seeking sequence variants or splice junctions. In the documented fixed RNA profiling workflow, synthetic ligated probes are sequenced rather than captured-transcript complementary DNA. Gene counts from that workflow do not provide unrestricted original transcript sequence. Source: https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/cell-ranger/7.2/getting-started/cr-flex-what-is-frp.
A barcode labels a reaction compartment and a UMI separates captured molecules from amplified copies, giving a gene-by-barcode table; a barcode does not guarantee one intact cell.

Single-nucleus sequencing samples nuclear RNA including unfinished transcripts with introns, whole cells also capture cytoplasmic messages; a mouse cortex study showed different recovery; not proof nuclei are better for tumours.
Dissociation can lose fragile cells; nuclei can come from frozen tissue; fixed-material probe methods count ligated probes and cannot reveal every variant or splice product.
A zero can be a missed molecule (dropout) rather than absence; ambient RNA contaminates profiles; a doublet combines cells or nuclei; correction does not certify every barcode.
A cluster groups similar profiles and does not prove malignancy, lineage or a clone; cancer-cell identification needs supporting evidence.
Thousands of cells from one biopsy are nested in one biological sample; splitting into two libraries does not create two patients; replicate-level aggregation is one approach.

Record compatible viable/frozen/fixed preparation, material used, chemistry, cell/nucleus recovery and quality/identity checks. Report a gene-by-barcode table with its UMI/read/probe counting unit. Cell calling, low-quality and doublet criteria are chemistry/version-specific. Selective recovery, sparse capture, ambient RNA, degradation and batch require validation; a platform name provides neither a complete census nor clinical validity.

A detection fraction uses the analysed profiles and a stated detection rule: it is not automatically the fraction of all cells in the original tissue. A profile with one immune-gene count but otherwise epithelial features is not thereby identified as an immune cell. Sparse recovery, ambient RNA and more than one contributing cell can complicate its interpretation. Check coherent marker evidence and the method of assignment; a mixture of markers does not by itself establish a new cell type. Pooling the counts from a selected set of profiles is pseudobulk. Five hundred nuclei from one biopsy can summarize that selected population, while the biopsy remains one biological specimen rather than five hundred independent patients.

Background correction estimates which part of a profile comes from free RNA in the preparation. SoupX's authors discuss deliberately overcorrecting contamination at the cost of removing a small amount of genuine signal. The estimated contamination and settings therefore need review; a corrected weak count or zero is not an infallible label of the molecule's origin.

Residual tumour here means cancer remaining in the sampled tissue after treatment. For residual-tumour research, first support malignant-cell identity, then ask which recovered states, target messages and immune profiles are present. A stress programme does not establish a genetic clone or explain survival. In Kim and colleagues' twenty-person triple-negative breast-cancer study, longitudinal exome data and single-cell DNA/RNA data in eight participants supported selection of pre-existing genotypes alongside expression reprogramming under the studied treatment. This is not a universal resistance mechanism. Compare the sampled region, time, preparation, recovery and analysis before attributing a difference to treatment; a missing cluster need not have been eliminated. In a separate fictional calculation, an input suspension truly containing 4 percent malignant nuclei gives an expectation of 240 among 6,000 retained profiles only if malignant and other nuclei have equal inclusion through recovery, capture and quality filtering. Tissue-area cellularity is a different denominator. The calculation is neither a yield forecast nor an adequacy cutoff.

Zheng and colleagues' 2017 droplet study grouped PCR duplicates by a shared partition barcode, UMI and gene assignment after its quality filters. In a fictional example, three qualifying reads in one such group count as one captured molecule; the same tag in another gene or partition is not automatically the same molecule. A UMI is a random sequence tag, rather than a globally unique name. Smith and colleagues showed that tag errors distort molecule estimates and described limits as the available tag diversity is used up. Retain the chemistry, grouping and error handling: the count is not a census of RNA originally present, proof of one cell per barcode or a protein measurement.

records.name: Cell lineage, identity and state
records.tldr: A cell’s ancestry, its type and its current activity answer different questions. Similar activity does not prove that two cells share a recent ancestor.
records.summary: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

notes: Reference atlases classify measured features. Barcodes or other validated tracing information add ancestry evidence, with their own labeling and sampling limits. Weinreb and colleagues combined expressed barcodes and transcriptomes over time in hematopoiesis; sister-cell analyses exposed fate biases that a single RNA snapshot missed. This does not identify an individual tumor’s origin from its expression profile.

Lim and colleagues studied normal and preneoplastic breast tissue from BRCA1 mutation carriers and found an expanded luminal-progenitor population. The expression profiles of BRCA1-associated tissue and basal breast tumours resembled normal luminal progenitors more than the other tested subsets. This supported a candidate population for transformation; it was not direct lineage tracing of an individual tumour. A luminal-progenitor-like RNA program does not by itself make a cancer hormone-receptor-positive.

Support a malignant-cell assignment with tissue context, a coherent marker panel, suitable normal references and quality checks, rather than one marker or cluster name. In five primary glioblastomas, Patel and colleagues profiled 430 cells and inferred broad chromosome alterations by averaging RNA expression along chromosomes against normal reference profiles. This was RNA-based inference, not a direct DNA copy count or a breast diagnostic rule. A flat inferred profile can miss a malignant cell lacking a detectable broad change; focal alterations and point mutations can also be missed. Matched DNA, pathology and spatial evidence can corroborate an assignment, but bulk DNA does not identify every RNA barcode. Mixed markers may reflect ambient RNA or doublets. In another fictional mixed sample, vimentin RNA could come from fibroblasts or a changed cancer-cell programme. Even cell-attributed expression of that marker alone does not establish invasion, resistance or ancestry. Keep uncertain assignments uncertain.

In a fictional set with separately established shared genetic ancestry, one cell is cycling and another is noncycling. Different activity labels do not require different ancestry. Conversely, two cells in the same RNA cluster need not belong to the same genetic clone. The origin of the ancestry label matters: expression resemblance alone does not establish it.

records.name: Cell composition confound (tumour versus stroma and immune cells)
records.tldr: Because a tumour sample is a mix of cancer, stromal and immune cells, a difference between two samples may only reflect a different mix of cells.
records.summary:
A tumour specimen can contain malignant, immune, stromal and normal cells. A difference in an aggregate molecular signal can reflect a changed mixture, changed expression within cells or both. That is different from a directly counted cell fraction or a density per sampled area, each of which also needs its denominator and sampled region.

Preparation can change what is recovered. Slyper and colleagues compared single-cell and single-nucleus profiling in matched tumour specimens and found similar cell types at sometimes different proportions. A recovered profile mixture is therefore not automatically the original tissue census. Deconvolution and purity models can help investigate contributions under assumptions; they do not certify the cell of origin of every signal or remove sampling differences.

notes: In a fictional assay using equal sampled areas and the same counting method, ten immune cells among fifty total cells is 20%, while ten among twenty is 50%. The immune count remains ten. Loss of other cells can raise the fraction without additional immune-cell entry; these observations alone do not establish recruitment, recognition or killing. This simple cell fraction is not the clinical stromal tumour-infiltrating-lymphocyte score, which has a different denominator.

A second invented comparison starts with ten cells in one square millimetre of viable edge from lesion L. Follow-up A counts ten in the same stated area and region of L, giving ten cells per square millimetre at both times under the supplied assumptions. Follow-up B counts ten in 0.2 square millimetres from an injured centre of lesion M, giving fifty per square millimetre. B does not show a rise within L. Retain the lesion, viable area, centre or edge, collection time, treatment context and counting method. An early sample can capture transient injury signals and a later one a changed surviving-cell mixture. Equal area does not make separate tissue pieces identical, and matched sampling alone still cannot establish recruitment causation.

Measurement layers ask different questions. Anatomical imaging describes structure; tracer imaging depends on the stated product and its distribution; immunohistochemistry localises a protein in sampled tissue; bulk RNA pools captured messages; receptor sequencing describes recovered sequences and their sampled abundances; and controlled recognition or killing assays test a specified function under their conditions. RNA abundance is not accessible surface protein. Formenti's lung-cancer radiation-plus-ipilimumab study used clinical, blood-repertoire and selected functional readouts together; none is a universal immune-success marker or a substitute for the other measurements.

An expression score requires compatible RNA input, locked preprocessing, genes, weights, reference, endpoint/horizon and software version. Existing data can be rescored without new tissue; acquiring RNA consumes material. Report categories, ranks, probabilities or unitless scores on their exact scale. Missing genes, batch, mixture and population shift undermine cutoffs; analytical, clinical and utility evidence remain separate.

An expression-program score has meaning within its algorithm and background. For a score formed by subtracting matched control-gene expression, zero need not mean that no program genes were detected. The 90th percentile places a result relative to a specified reference; it does not mean that 90 percent of cells express the program or that a pathway is 90 percent active. Changing the genes, preprocessing, controls or reference can change the scale, so retain them with the method and version.

records.name: Notch signalling
records.tldr: Notch receptors can relay signals between contacting cells. The effect depends on the receptor, ligand, alteration and tissue; receiving a signal does not by itself prove growth dependence.
records.summary:
A ligand-bearing sender, receptor amount, received signal and growth dependence are separate observations. Locate malignant, vessel and other neighboring cells before assigning a Notch mechanism. Ligand on a vessel is not evidence that the tumor received the signal, and total receptor is different from a released nuclear intracellular domain.

Common contact-dependent Notch signaling begins when Delta-like or Jagged ligand on one cell engages a receptor on a neighbor. Ligand-regulated extracellular cleavage permits subsequent gamma-secretase-mediated membrane cleavage; the released Notch intracellular domain, NICD, can enter the nucleus and work with transcriptional partners. This route differs from an RTK phosphorylation relay and omits receptor maturation and sender mechanics.

Weng found activating NOTCH1 changes in extracellular heterodimerization or PEST regions in more than half of the studied T-ALLs. Agrawal identified predicted inactivating alterations in head-and-neck squamous tumors, suggesting a tumor-suppressor role there. An uncharacterized allele inherits neither direction from the pathway name; tissue, cell identity and alteration effect matter.

A fictional T-ALL culture with high nuclear NICD without a ligand-bearing neighbor, and lower NICD after gamma-secretase blockade, supports a ligand-independent activation hypothesis. A contact-blocking experiment that lowers NICD without changing growth instead supports reduced received signaling without demonstrating a growth requirement. Control general toxicity, contact conditions, independent pathway perturbations and compensation. Gamma-secretase also processes other proteins; responsive HES/HEY RNA and nuclear staining need validated assays and are not universal eligibility cutoffs.
