Stoeck 2014 identified NOTCH1 or NOTCH2 rearrangements in six of 66 triple-negative breast cancers. The studied NOTCH1 rearrangements retained gamma-secretase-dependent release of the active intracellular domain, and high-active-NOTCH1 models responded to inhibition in culture and xenografts, including tested paclitaxel combinations. A NOTCH2 fusion encoded an active intracellular product that bypassed the cleavage step and its model resisted that inhibitor. Position alone was not sufficient: a NOTCH1-rearranged line with low active-NOTCH1 signal also resisted. Both the actual active product and model conditions matter. The experiment does not make all activated Notch equivalent, validate a universal staining cutoff or establish a clinical selection rule.

Notch is also used by normal tissues. Van Es and colleagues found that removing the shared Notch transcriptional effector or blocking gamma-secretase converted proliferating intestinal crypt cells into differentiated goblet cells; the study also tested adenomas in Apc-mutant mice. Rangarajan and colleagues found that keratinocyte-specific Notch1 deletion produced epidermal hyperplasia and altered differentiation markers, while their primary-keratinocyte experiments separated growth arrest from differentiation responses. These defined intestinal and skin experiments do not make Notch a tumour-only switch or assign every receptor, tissue and inhibitor the same effect.

Clinical safety can constrain a pathway intervention even when its output is inhibited. In Messersmith and colleagues' 2015 phase I study of PF-03084014 in advanced solid tumours, the recommended phase II dose was lower than the estimated maximum tolerated dose because it had a better safety profile with comparable NOTCH-related target inhibition. Treatment-related events included diarrhoea and rash. The trial does not prove that each event was caused by the normal intestinal or skin mechanism, nor provide a universal safe dose for Notch inhibitors.

Hellström and colleagues perturbed Dll4/Notch1 signalling in mouse retinal vessels. Inhibiting the route increased tip-cell formation; the authors interpreted signalling between endothelial neighbours as restricting tip-cell numbers relative to stalk cells. Tip and stalk describe roles in a growing vessel, rather than cancer cells assigned a simple growth-on or growth-off state. These experiments do not establish the state of a human tumour from a pathway label.

records.name: Wnt / β-catenin
records.tldr: Canonical Wnt signalling regulates beta-catenin and gene activity. Its output, dependence on a Wnt ligand and effects on cell growth are separate questions.
records.summary:
Canonical pathway output, dependence on secreted Wnt, growth dependence and clinical response are separate claims. Nuclear beta-catenin can reflect pathway signaling, whereas total beta-catenin also includes adhesion functions. Lower AXIN2 RNA supports an output effect with suitable controls, not selective killing or patient benefit. Wnt routes that do not use beta-catenin are outside this canonical readout.

Canonical Wnt uses Frizzled with LRP5/6 co-receptor machinery. Without an effective signal, the Axin/APC-organized destruction machinery and sequential kinase steps promote beta-catenin degradation; signaling can change that control and allow nuclear regulation with partners. PORCN supplies a lipid modification required for proper Wnt secretion in the studied systems. Blocking that upstream step need not overcome a downstream escape from destruction control.

Two fictional cultures have nuclear beta-catenin. Secretion blockade reduces the nuclear signal in culture A but not in culture B, where downstream bypass is stipulated. A supports a ligand-dependent hypothesis; B illustrates how an upstream block can leave a downstream output intact. The symbols represent qualitative readouts, not protein counts or a real drug dataset. Neither pattern alone establishes selective killing; measure viability and control intervention specificity.

Assays can measure localization, AXIN2 RNA or a defined transcriptional reporter, before and after a specified perturbation. Preservation, composition, global transcription effects, model validation and tissue consumption matter; there is no universal Wnt-high treatment cutoff. In Rodon's phase 1 WNT974 study of 94 people with advanced solid tumors, AXIN2 fell in many paired biopsies while no RECIST responses were observed. Target-related output and tumor response must therefore be reported separately, alongside safety rather than a claim of demonstrated benefit.

Normal bone also uses Wnt-related signalling. Gong and colleagues linked LRP5 mutations to osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome, found reduced bone mass in carriers, detected LRP5 in osteoblasts and demonstrated canonical Wnt signalling through it in culture. These genetic and experimental findings concern bone accrual; they do not estimate the fracture risk of every Wnt inhibitor. In the WNT974 trial, the authors considered dysgeusia likely to result from on-target Wnt inhibition, but a maximum tolerated dose was not established. Safety findings, pathway-output changes and antitumour benefit remain distinct.

LIN28A is an RNA-binding regulator of microRNA processing and translation, as described in its reviewed human UniProt entry. It is not a Wnt ligand or Frizzled receptor. A list containing these different gene products does not establish coordinated activity or their presence in one genetic clone. Assign an intercellular signal to its sender and receiver; shared malignant ancestry is a separate claim.

records.name: Ferroptosis & regulated cell death
records.tldr: Ferroptosis is a form of cell death involving iron-dependent membrane-lipid damage. General oxidative stress or one positive marker does not establish this mechanism.
records.summary: Ferroptosis involves iron-dependent membrane-lipid peroxidation and death. Cystine uptake through system xc- can support cysteine and glutathione availability; it does not transport glutathione itself. GPX4 uses glutathione to reduce lipid hydroperoxides, while FSP1 provides a parallel coenzyme-Q-associated defence. Dependence on these routes varies with the model and cellular conditions. Establishing the mechanism requires appropriately controlled measurements of death, lipid damage, iron dependence and rescue, with complementary perturbations. Findings in persistent or mesenchymal model cells do not establish a universal vulnerability or a treatment recommendation. Necrotic appearance, danger signals and adaptive antitumour immunity are separate questions.

GPX4 uses glutathione to reduce lipid hydroperoxides to lipid alcohols. FSP1 provides a parallel coenzyme-Q radical-trapping defence; it does not replace every GPX4 function or describe the whole protection network. Protein abundance alone does not measure protective activity or predict compound sensitivity.

Assigning ferroptosis needs convergent measurements of death, lipid damage preceding death, iron dependence and appropriately controlled rescue. Independent genetic and chemical perturbations strengthen attribution; rescue alone is not complete proof. Probe chemistry, concentration, nutrients, cell density and observation time can alter results. A lipid-probe ratio and death fraction are different outputs, with no universal diagnostic staining threshold. Live death and rescue tests consume viable model material. Specify lipid-probe oxidation ratios and independently measured death percentages over a stated interval; a marker snapshot does not reconstruct the full causal sequence.

A culture with abundant GPX4, a general oxidation signal and no death has not demonstrated ferroptosis. Cell-line and xenograft vulnerabilities do not establish tolerable exposure, selective cancer killing or benefit in patients. Alternative defences can confer resistance, so a strong antioxidant programme is not automatically a treatment vulnerability.

Hangauer 2017 investigated reversible drug-tolerant persister states across specified cancer-cell and drug models. Surviving the original treatment could coexist with increased GPX4 dependence; this was not necessarily permanent genetic resistance. The breast model BT474 is HER2-positive, not a triple-negative model. In the mouse relapse experiment, A375 melanoma cells had genetic GPX4 loss, with ferrostatin protection withdrawn while dabrafenib and trametinib continued. Prevented relapse in that setting was not systemic treatment with a GPX4 inhibitor: the authors noted poor systemic pharmacokinetics of RSL3 and ML210. These experiments do not establish a tolerable human window or universal persister vulnerability.

A fictional GPX4 experiment combines lipid oxidation before death, rescue by an iron chelator and a lipid-radical trap, and a corresponding phenotype after an independent genetic perturbation. These observations converge on an iron-dependent lipid-damage explanation; none alone proves it. Include vehicle, rescue-only and an unrelated death condition because rescue compounds can affect other processes. Survival of an otherwise matched FSP1-high comparison is compatible with a parallel defence; directly testing that defence is needed before assigning compensation to it. Energy production, a general oxidation dye and an antioxidant transcript are different measurements and cannot substitute for this causal sequence.
records.analogy: Ferroptosis is rust. Iron plus oxygen eats through the cell's membranes unless an antioxidant crew (GPX4) keeps repainting them. Cells that changed shape to dodge chemotherapy have thinner paint.
interventions: xCT inhibitors, cyst(e)inase, sulfasalazine repurposing (early trials)
Radiotherapy and IFN-γ from T cells induce lipid peroxidation
BH3 mimetics (venetoclax) exploit apoptosis; MCL-1 inhibitors in development

records.name: KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway
records.tldr: KEAP1-NRF2 regulates cellular stress defences. Protection, metabolic dependence and treatment response need separate tests in the relevant cancer and conditions.
records.summary:
KEAP1 helps a CUL3-containing ubiquitin-ligase system regulate NRF2 turnover. Loss of relevant KEAP1 function can stabilise NRF2 and increase antioxidant, detoxification and drug-export programmes. A gene alteration or high RNA signal alone does not establish its functional direction, the affected cells or a treatment response.

Singh 2006 identified KEAP1 mutations in ten of 54 non-small-cell lung cancer samples, including primary tumours and pleural fluid. Among six mutation-bearing primary tumours assessed for the remaining locus, five had loss of heterozygosity. The cell experiments supported increased NRF2-related activity and drug-resistance mechanisms in those systems, rather than resistance to every therapy.

Romero 2017 used gene editing and metabolic experiments in KRAS-driven lung cancer models: Keap1 loss promoted tumour growth and created a glutaminolysis vulnerability in the tested systems. A protective programme can therefore coexist with a dependence on a different supply route. The randomised phase 2 KEAPSAKE registry records 40 actual participants and termination for lack of clinical benefit from the telaglenastat combination strategy. A preclinical dependence is not an approved treatment or a universal predictor of benefit.

Ten mutation-bearing samples round to 19 per cent, not a universal lung-cancer prevalence. Five of six tested mutation-bearing primary tumours had locus loss; do not assign biallelic loss to all ten samples. Romero separately described KEAP1 alterations in about 20 per cent of KRAS-mutant lung adenocarcinomas. These populations and denominators differ. KEAP1-mutant-versus-normal-cell viability comparisons are not matched isogenic proof that one alteration caused every chemotherapy response.

Protection and dependence are experiment-specific directions. If removing a verified defence makes a defined stress more lethal, that supports protection under that stress. If removing the defence or a supply route reduces survival relative to an appropriate matched comparison, that supports a conditional dependence; it need not mean every unstressed cell dies. In a fictional culture, high antioxidant RNA plus probe-associated death establishes neither NRF2-driven killing nor ferroptosis. Test the alteration's effect on NRF2 turnover or nuclear localisation and output, then use independent perturbation and restoration to examine the survival mechanism. CUL3 works with other adaptors, and a compound suppressing protein production broadly does not isolate NRF2. A genetic intervention also needs controls, rather than being automatically specific.

ClinicalTrials.gov records KEAPSAKE, NCT04265534, as a randomised, double-blind phase 2 comparison of telaglenastat or placebo added to carboplatin, pemetrexed and pembrolizumab for selected metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC with KEAP1/NRF2 alterations. The record last updated in September 2022 reports actual enrollment 40, status terminated and the stated reason lack of clinical benefit. This is registry status, not a peer-reviewed effect estimate or proof that every glutaminase strategy fails. Model activity, eligibility, acceptable exposure and clinical benefit remain different questions.

Vartanian and colleagues examined brusatol in the KEAP1-mutant lung-cancer line A549. Protein profiling and measurements of newly synthesised proteins supported broad inhibition of protein synthesis, with NRF2 falling among many proteins. Cytotoxicity across additional cancer cell lines was not restricted to KEAP1-NRF2 activity. A lower NRF2 signal after this compound therefore does not isolate NRF2 inhibition as the cause of death. Check general translation early and use independently controlled perturbations before attributing a survival effect to the proposed defence.
records.analogy: A large fire service could reflect frequent fires, effective protection or dependence on a particular fuel supply. Counting equipment alone cannot distinguish those explanations; the corresponding cellular questions require activity, perturbation and survival measurements.
interventions: Investigate the exact alteration, NRF2 turnover or localisation and relevant target outputs before assigning pathway activity.
Test a proposed protective or metabolic dependence with defined perturbations, appropriate comparators and survival measurements.

records.name: Ubiquitin-proteasome system & protein homeostasis
records.tldr: Ubiquitin can change a protein's interactions, location or fate. Some tags support proteasomal destruction; tagging alone does not establish completed degradation.
records.summary: E1 enzymes activate ubiquitin, E2 enzymes carry it and E3 ligases help select substrates and assemble modifications. Chain architecture and cellular context influence the result; ubiquitination is not universally a destruction signal. Deubiquitinases can remove or remodel tags, and proteasomal degradation is a later process that needs its own evidence. A protein can fall because synthesis changes, cells are lost or degradation increases, so abundance alone does not identify the route. In targeted-degradation experiments, target binding, E3 recruitment, protein loss, proteasome dependence and sustained cellular effects are distinct observations. Proteasome inhibitors and recruited-degradation strategies intervene at different steps; mechanistic measurements do not by themselves establish clinical benefit.

Suitable tagged cargo can be unfolded by ATP-dependent proteasomal machinery and broken into fragments, while ubiquitin is removed and reused. Other ubiquitin signals organise interactions rather than destruction, and yeast experiments show overlapping chain functions. Lysosomal autophagy and proteasomal breakdown are distinct routes.

Protein abundance reflects synthesis and removal. Measure named-substrate decay over time with synthesis, handling and viability controls; restoration of an E3 adaptor can strengthen attribution without proving direct binding or global proteasome failure. Catalytic activity per time, ubiquitinated-cargo intensity and protein lifetime in hours are different readouts. KEAP1 is one CUL3 adaptor for NRF2, so a CUL3 change cannot uniquely identify that substrate. Pulse labelling or a controlled temporary synthesis block can help estimate turnover but may cause stress. Independent perturbation and restoration help distinguish a selected-substrate effect from a secondary response; enzyme engagement alone does not establish selective killing.

In a randomised trial of 669 people with relapsed myeloma after one to three prior therapies, bortezomib prolonged median time to progression compared with high-dose dexamethasone: 6.22 versus 3.49 months. This historical clinical result does not make an arbitrary E3 variant or abundant protein a predictive treatment biomarker.

Proteasomal degradation commonly handles individual suitable proteins, whereas lysosomal macroautophagy can deliver aggregates, organelles and portions of cytoplasm. This is a distinction of machinery and typical cargo, not an absolute partition: ubiquitinated material can also be recognised by autophagy adaptors such as p62. A tagged protein, an autophagic membrane marker and disappearance of a named cargo are different observations. Bortezomib's relapsed-myeloma trial result does not predict a hydroxychloroquine result in pancreatic cancer, and blocking both routes does not by itself demonstrate selective harm to malignant cells.

records.name: Lipid synthesis, uptake & cholesterol
records.tldr: Cells can make, import, store and reuse lipids. The route they use and their dependence on it vary with the cell and conditions.
records.summary: Lipid metabolism includes synthesis, uptake, storage, membrane remodelling and oxidation. Cholesterol regulation and fatty-acid regulation overlap but are not interchangeable. Identify the SREBP member, cellular compartment and measured output rather than treating a transcript, precursor, nuclear fragment, sterol amount and synthesis rate as the same observation. SCAP-SREBP transport responds to endoplasmic reticulum cholesterol in the cited cell experiments. The mevalonate pathway supplies sterols and nonsterol products, including substrates for protein prenylation. Rescue by mevalonate therefore cannot uniquely identify cholesterol as the limiting product. Transcript abundance, lipid abundance, labelled production and a controlled survival-dependence experiment answer different questions. Results from a particular cell model or mouse experiment do not establish a universal tumour vulnerability or a preferred diet or treatment.

notes: SCAP and local endoplasmic-reticulum sterol conditions regulate transport of membrane-bound SREBP to the Golgi. Processing releases a fragment that enters the nucleus and regulates lipid synthesis and uptake. Sufficient local sterol supply can retain the complex in the ER; total cellular cholesterol and SREBP RNA do not measure this processing.

In the fictional supply experiment, nuclear SREBP-2 and uptake messages respond to lipid-poor medium; external lipid supply can reduce the response and compensate for synthesis perturbation. Record medium composition, density, timing and viability before assigning dependence. A supply-sensitive state does not establish the response of a person's tumour. Assess precursor and nuclear regulator, responsive transcripts, cellular sterols and uptake separately from labelled synthesis rates. Use controlled supplementation to test the proposed bottleneck; total amount does not specify production or local sensing. Lower synthesis does not itself show that a compound bound its target, and a medium effect does not identify uptake as its cause. An uncharacterised SCAP or MTOR variant needs evidence for its proposed functional effect; a gene name alone assigns neither activation nor loss of function.

In transgenic mice expressing a truncated SREBP-2 construct, Horton and colleagues observed preferential activation of cholesterol synthesis over fatty-acid synthesis in liver and adipose tissue, contrasting it with earlier SREBP-1a results. They separately measured transcripts and synthesis using labelled water. These are relative effects in a named experimental system, not exclusive duties of each family member or proof that a transcript measurement equals flux. Precursor location and nuclear processing require their own measurements.

Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase upstream in the mevalonate pathway, which supplies cholesterol and nonsterol products. In Freed-Pastor and colleagues' breast-cancer 3D cultures, geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate partially rescued an invasive phenotype after mutant-p53 depletion or simvastatin treatment. This illustrates why mevalonate rescue alone cannot uniquely attribute an effect to cholesterol. It does not identify every relevant metabolite, establish a universal cancer dependency or show that a statin perturbation reproduces every change in SCAP-SREBP regulation.

HMG-CoA reductase makes mevalonate and is inhibited by statins. The downstream pathway branches: farnesyl pyrophosphate, FPP, feeds sterol synthesis through squalene and GGPP production as well as supplying protein prenylation; geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, GGPP, supplies another prenylation route. Farnesyl and geranylgeranyl lipid modifications help position specified RAS- and RHO-family proteins, respectively. Cholesterol is a membrane component and a precursor of steroid hormones. Cholesterol amount, sterol synthesis and the whole mevalonate pathway are therefore different measurements. SCAP-SREBP sterol sensing regulates synthesis and uptake, but its activity, pathway transcripts, metabolite supply and dependence must each be established in the tested cells and medium.

Freed-Pastor 2012 studied mutant-p53 breast cancer cells in three-dimensional culture, with different outcomes in two triple-negative lines. Depleting mutant p53 reduced invasive behaviour in MDA-MB-231 but did not make it form ordered hollow acini; MDA-MB-468 could acquire a more ordered, hollow architecture. Statins reduced invasion in the former and caused growth inhibition with extensive death in the latter, rather than exactly reproducing every p53-depletion phenotype. Mutant-p53 depletion reduced mevalonate-pathway expression, and mevalonate add-back opposed several statin effects. This supports a pathway contribution in the studied systems without isolating cholesterol. The whole paper also examined growth, death and xenograft growth; it was not solely an architecture experiment, and none of these results established patient treatment benefit.

The branch experiments further narrowed an invasive-morphology question in MDA-MB-231. Blocking the geranylgeranylation branch had a larger effect than the tested sterol-branch block, and GGPP partly restored invasive growth after mutant-p53 depletion or statin treatment. That is not evidence that GGPP rescues inhibition of the transferase itself, nor that every effect in both cell lines was entirely explained by one metabolite. The authors allowed contributions from other products. In a fictional supply comparison, synthesis falls under an inhibitor in both lipid-poor and lipid-rich medium, but growth slows mainly in the former while import is stipulated to compensate in the latter. Equal engagement with different growth outcomes is compatible with environmental supply; it is not a measurement of supply or dependence in a person's tumour.

In the selected SREBP-2 route, the precursor spans a membrane and its gene-regulating end faces the cytosol. SCAP escorts the membrane-bound precursor from endoplasmic reticulum through transport vesicles to Golgi membranes. Cleavage releases the regulatory fragment into cytosol before nuclear entry; it does not carry the whole precursor, SCAP or the vesicle into the nucleus. Local sterol sensing and Insig-associated retention regulate this transport. A schematic of the route supplies neither a universal sterol threshold nor a measured transcription rate.
records.analogy: A factory that must build its own walls. Normal adult tissue buys wall panels from a supplier (dietary fat); cancer reopens its own panel plant (FASN) and, when it lands in a fat depot, simply strips panels off the buildings next door.

records.name: Proteomics instruments and affinity platforms
records.tldr: Machines that measure thousands of proteins at once from tissue or blood, used to find drug targets and early-detection markers.
records.summary: Mass spectrometry (Thermo Fisher Orbitrap Astral, Bruker timsTOF, SCIEX ZenoTOF) and affinity-based platforms (Olink/Thermo Fisher Explore, SomaLogic/Standard BioTools SomaScan, Alamar NULISA, Nautilus and Quantum-Si single-molecule approaches) deliver deep proteomes; UK Biobank's 50,000-participant Olink dataset and CPTAC's tumour proteogenomics illustrate the discovery value. Clinical proteomic tests remain few.

records.name: Phosphorylation
records.tldr: Adding phosphate can change a protein’s behavior in several ways. The site and cellular context determine whether a measured change indicates activation, inhibition or something else.
records.summary: Protein kinases commonly transfer phosphate from ATP to a substrate, producing ADP. Protein phosphatases remove phosphate by hydrolysis without regenerating ATP. A modification can affect catalysis, binding, localization or interactions; sites on one protein can have different functions. Src experiments demonstrated an inhibitory tail-phosphorylation mechanism in their defined preparation, so phosphorylation should not be treated as universal activation.

A phosphatase uses water to release phosphate and restore the hydroxyl group, without making ATP. These reactions modify a site on an existing molecule and do not measure how much protein is present.

records.name: Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
records.tldr: Staining a tissue slice with antibodies so a protein shows up in colour under the microscope.
records.summary: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.

notes: There is no universal IHC scoring scale or positivity threshold. Retain antibody clone, retrieval and detection method, controls, eligible cells, subcellular location, intensity, distribution and intended use. A research stain does not automatically replace a clinical selection assay.

An H-score under the intensity-weighted convention is weak-cell percentage plus twice moderate-cell percentage plus three times strong-cell percentage, on a 0 to 300 scale. Fictional example: 50 unstained, 10 weak, 20 moderate and 20 strong cells out of 100 give 50% positive and H-score 110. Neither is a molecule count.

Bulk receptor abundance and staining mainly on blood vessels can both be correct: one measures a mixture and the other locates signal. Neither establishes target accessibility or treatment benefit. Staining also does not establish protein activity or cancer-cell dependence on that protein.

IHC makes selected proteins visible through antibody binding and signal development in a prepared section. Specificity, retrieval, detection, positive controls, internal controls and background matter. Nuclear and membrane signals answer different questions. Multiplex fluorescence adds markers but still needs validated antibody performance and cell-boundary assignment.

In the conventional Allred scheme, proportion categories are 0 for no positive cells, 1 for less than 1%, 2 for 1% to 10%, 3 for 11% to 33%, 4 for 34% to 66% and 5 for 67% to 100%. Intensity is 0 for absent staining or 1, 2 and 3 for weak, moderate and strong staining. The total is 0 or 2 to 8. In a fictional separate example, 30% positive cells with moderate staining give 3 + 2 = 5. These integer bins are a named convention, not a universal positivity rule.

Equal H-scores can conceal different intensity distributions. A negative clinical category does not establish zero protein molecules. HER2 and hormone-receptor assays have marker-specific reporting rules; current CAP breast reporting retains percentage and intensity even when an optional composite score is given.

A useful IHC result identifies the block, fixation and section, antibody clone, retrieval and detection system, eligible cells and scored compartment. Cutting and staining use finite tissue. Report the percentage, intensity, location and named scoring scale, together with expected-positive tissue, relevant internal controls and background assessment. Poor preservation, nonspecific binding, few eligible cells, heterogeneous staining and observer variation can limit interpretation. Validation must fit the assay and its intended use; a research measurement is not automatically a clinical selection test.

Staining recognises an antibody-defined molecular feature, or epitope, rather than automatically proving a complete functioning protein. In an invented repair-gene example, weaker staining in identified cancer cells than in normal neighbours supports a cell-specific signal difference if the controls are adequate. The antibody may recognise a fragment or more than one protein form, so this does not give the amount of intact useful repair protein. The relevant form and current repair need suitable measurements of their own. One validated method can sometimes answer several questions, but measuring one property does not establish every other one.

records.tldr: Exome sequencing targets mostly protein-coding exons; genome sequencing samples DNA more broadly. Both have coverage and detection limits.
records.summary: With suitable preparation and analysis, WGS can reveal structural variants, mutational signatures (HRD, APOBEC, tobacco), whole-genome doubling, and non-coding drivers. Used by national programmes (Genomics England, Hartwig) and for neoantigen prediction in personalised vaccines. Suitable long-read sequencing (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore) can help resolve complex rearrangements and methylation in one run.

Check the platform, preparation, validated regions and alteration classes before interpreting a negative result.

records.name: Gene fusion
records.tldr: A gene fusion joins sequences from different genes. Its RNA product, protein consequence and treatment relevance each need evidence.
records.summary:
A gene fusion joins sequences from different genes. Reports may describe an underlying DNA rearrangement, an expressed RNA junction or a predicted fusion protein. These are different observations: an expressed junction does not by itself establish the complete DNA structure, protein function or growth dependence. Some kinase fusions drive cancers; a candidate call can also be nonfunctional or an analytical artefact.

RNA sequencing can identify expressed fusion junctions, so whole-genome sequencing is not the only fusion-capable method. Stransky and colleagues analysed RNA sequencing from nearly 7,000 TCGA tumour samples and filtered and reviewed candidate kinase fusions. Their study-specific criteria included a predicted in-frame coding sequence and a retained kinase domain; those criteria are not a universal clinical calling rule.

Interpret the exact assay's covered regions, preparation, detection limits and supporting evidence. A negative result is limited by that workflow. A fusion involving a drug-associated gene does not automatically establish an active protein, sensitivity to that drug or patient benefit.

Point mutations in these genes are a different alteration class. Their functional and clinical effects need their own evidence; being different from a fusion does not make them passengers. The practical rule is that a driver-negative adenocarcinoma, especially in a never smoker, has not been fully tested until a fusion-capable assay has been run (Lindeman 2018).

records.name: Mutational signature
records.tldr: An inferred pattern of mutations that supports hypotheses about the processes that produced them. Its interpretation depends on the data, comparison patterns and method.
records.summary:
A mutational signature is a distribution over mutation categories inferred from a catalog of calls. It does not attach an observed cause to every mutation. Several processes can overlap, some causes remain unknown, and a classifier of BRCA-related repair deficiency is not a model of a patient's probability of drug response. Its endpoint and validation population must be named.

Single-base substitutions change one base, doublet substitutions change adjacent bases, and indels insert or delete sequence. In a fictional four-category exercise, template A has percentages 40, 30, 20, 10 and B has 30, 40, 20, 10. For 100 mutations, a 50/50 mixture gives 35, 35, 20, 10; a 60/40 mixture gives 36, 34, 20, 10. The close reconstructions illustrate ambiguity; these are arithmetic examples, not fitted SBS3 data or observed biological results.

HRDetect combines six weighted features, including microhomology-associated deletions, substitution signatures 3 and 8, rearrangement signatures 3 and 5 and a scar index. It is not simply an SBS3-positive call. In the original study, applying genome-trained weights to exome-like data reduced sensitivity to 46.8%; retraining improved it to 73% while adding calls not made by the genome model. Missing rearrangements and sparse substitutions are consequential, so panel, exome and whole-genome implementations require separate validation, uncertainty and fit checks.

Roberts analyzed 954,247 mutations across 2,680 exomes from 14 cancer types; the APOBEC pattern reached 68% of mutations in some samples, not in every breast cancer. HRDetect reported 98.7% sensitivity and 124 high-scoring tumors among 560 breast cancers, about 22%, under its study definition. That selected cohort estimate is not a population prevalence or a clinical response probability. DNA quality, variant-calling errors, signature competition, catalog and software versions remain part of interpretation.

records.name: DNA
records.tldr: DNA stores sequence information. Its packaging, copying and use as a template for RNA are different processes.
records.summary: DNA contains nucleotide chains with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases A, T, C and G. Complementary A–T and C–G pairing joins antiparallel strands. Nuclear chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins as chromatin; nucleosomes organize DNA around histones. Mitochondria carry a separate genome. A gene is a functional region within DNA, rather than an entire chromosome. Replication copies DNA, while transcription produces RNA from a selected template. Packaging and gene presence do not establish active transcription or a functional protein.

The damage response is another observation: an assay for gamma-H2AX measures a histone modification associated with a response, rather than reading a variant sequence. Experimental work also shows that this signal is not an unambiguous count of double-strand breaks. A sequencing variant call, a lesion assay and a damage-response stain answer different questions; one is not a count of the others.

For a short invented duplex, 5-prime ATCG 3-prime pairs with 3-prime TAGC 5-prime. The paired bases sit between sugar-phosphate backbones, and nuclear DNA can wrap around histone cores to form nucleosomes. A gene occupies a region of DNA, not the entire chromosome. A packaging cartoon does not establish one universal 30 nm fibre, an X-shaped chromosome at every stage, copy number or gene activity.

records.name: Gene amplification and copy-number change
records.tldr: Cancer cells often have extra copies of a growth gene (amplification) or have lost copies of a protective one (deletion), rather than a spelling change within the gene. Extra copies of HER2 or MYCN are classic examples that change treatment.
records.summary: Amplification (detected by FISH, ISH or NGS copy-number calls) can increase gene dosage and expression: HER2 in breast and gastric cancer, MYCN in high-risk neuroblastoma, MET amplification as a resistance route to EGFR inhibitors, CCNE1 in ovarian and gastric cancer, MDM2 in liposarcoma, CDK4 in glioma. Deletions remove tumour suppressors: del(17p)/TP53 in CLL and myeloma (predicting chemo-resistance), CDKN2A/B in glioma (defining grade 4), MTAP (creating a PRMT5 vulnerability), 9p21 loss linked to immunotherapy resistance. Loss of heterozygosity and larger chromosome changes contribute to some method-defined genomic-scar scores. Their clinical interpretation depends on the exact test, cancer and treatment setting; a copy state alone does not establish current repair function or drug benefit.

notes: Total copy count, allele identity, RNA abundance and protein activity are separate measurements. Purity, ploidy and the assay’s definition affect copy calls. Fehrmann and colleagues related copy number to expression after modelling shared transcriptional components in large datasets; that association does not promise a fixed protein increase, target dependence or treatment benefit in a particular tumour.
Total copy number counts copies of a region; allele-specific copy number estimates the contributions of the distinguishable sequence versions A and B.
1+1 is two copies with both versions; 1+0 is one copy with LOH (deletion); 2+0 is copy-neutral LOH (two copies, one version); 2+1 is three copies with both versions retained.
LOH is not synonymous with deletion: copy-neutral LOH can follow loss plus duplication or recombination; a gain does not necessarily erase either version.

Major and minor counts are the larger and smaller allelic contributions; minor of zero supports LOH under the model; they do not identify parental origin or assign a mutation to a copy; phasing needs suitable evidence.
Local copy count differs from ploidy; relative signal can fit different purity and ploidy pairs; fractional counts can reflect mixture or subclonal states.

Methods combine relative coverage with allele balance at informative heterozygous sites, segment the genome and fit states; a matched normal helps; a total-copy profile alone cannot separate 1+1 from 2+0; homozygous sites are uninformative.
Copy state does not establish phase, gene inactivity, expression, dependency or drug response; bulk fits can hide subpopulations and unsampled lesions.
Fictional teaching exercise: Two A copies and no B copies under an adequate model is copy-neutral LOH: not deleted and not proven inactive.

For copy-state analysis, record tumour and suitable normal DNA, extraction consumption, relative depth and informative-site balance, segmentation, total/major/minor copies and purity/ploidy uncertainty. Reanalysis alone needs no tissue. Low purity, uninformative sites and ambiguous fits limit inference; amplification and functional-loss criteria are method-specific.

In a cancer copy-number report, an amplicon is an amplified DNA segment and can contain several genes. TCGA described multiple HER2-amplicon-associated genes, including GRB7, in its breast-cancer analysis. A regional gain does not identify every included gene as a driver or guarantee the same multiplication of RNA or protein; allele-specific state, expression, location and functional importance remain separate questions.

records.name: Copy number alteration (CNA)
records.tldr: A copy number alteration is a stretch of DNA that a tumour has gained extra copies of or lost, from a single gene to a whole chromosome arm.
records.summary: Copy number variation is a form of structural variation in which sections of the genome are duplicated or deleted (Wikipedia); in tumours the acquired form is called a somatic copy number alteration. Arm-level and focal events are called from arrays or sequencing, and GISTIC2.0 is the standard method for finding regions amplified or deleted more often than chance across a cohort. CNA is one of TCGA's core data types and a modality in most multi-omic models.

records.name: Tumour purity
records.tldr: Tumour purity is the fraction of cells in a sample that are actually cancer cells rather than normal, immune or stromal cells.
records.summary: Aran, Sirota and Butte's pan-cancer analysis of TCGA estimated the proportion of cancer cells in each sample by several methods (pathologist counts, copy number, expression and methylation based estimators) and showed purity varies widely between and within cancer types and confounds molecular comparisons. Bulk sequencing measures the whole mixture, so a low-purity sample can look like a different tumour; models trained on bulk data inherit this.

notes: Purity estimates and ploidy fits belong to the tested region and method. A pathology estimate of malignant-cell proportion and a sequencing model fit can disagree. Ploidy is a genome-wide average; local copy number can differ. Several purity-ploidy combinations may explain similar data.

Idealised arithmetic assumes diploid normal cells, diploid cancer cells and one mutant copy in every cancer cell: at purity 80%, 50% and 20%, expected variant allele fractions are 40%, 25% and 10%. A one-copy cancer-cell deletion yields mixed average copy numbers 1.2, 1.5 and 1.8 respectively. Copy changes and subclones alter these relationships.

Purity describes the malignant-cell share of the sampled cell mixture; a DNA-based estimate must account for how many genome copies the cells contribute. Ploidy is the average cancer-cell genome copy number. The marble-mixture analogy stops where local copy number and subclonal differences make each cell contribution unequal.

ASCAT reported aneuploidy above 2.7 genome copies in 45% of its early breast cancer series and near-triploid basal-like genomes consistent with loss followed by duplication. A separate advanced-cancer study identified whole-genome doubling in nearly 30% of 9,692 patients. These populations are different. A region with three copies can be a relative loss against a four-copy baseline, while exceeding a normal diploid count.

Nine pathologists estimated tumour-cell content on 47 lung tumour slides; 33% of estimates differed from manually counted content by at least three categories, mostly 10 percentage-points wide. ASCAT and ABSOLUTE jointly infer purity and ploidy from allelic copy number and related signals. Several fits, subclonal changes and low tumour content can complicate interpretation; a model fit is not a direct count.

Copy-number-based genomic scars depend on segmentation and interpretation of purity and ploidy. Popova used ploidy-specific large-scale transition cutoffs in basal-like breast cancers. Telli evaluated a combined loss-of-heterozygosity, telomeric-imbalance and large-scale-transition score of at least 42 or BRCA1/2 mutation in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant TNBC trials. This does not create a universal HRD threshold or prove current repair function or treatment benefit from a fit alone.

Fictional near-diploid example: 18% variant allele fraction is compatible with one mutant copy in every malignant cell at 36% purity, assuming diploid normal cells and no local copy change. It does not prove clonality. At 90% purity, the same VAF would need a different explanation such as subclonality or copy-number context. A negative low-purity result can reflect limited detection, not biological absence.

Sequencing purity belongs to the region used for extraction. Tumour-bed cellularity is an area-based residual cancer burden input, while plasma tumour fraction concerns circulating DNA. Sparse residual malignant cells can make post-treatment sequencing difficult; retain the tested block and laboratory-specific detection limits.

A pathology estimate uses the represented slide region, while a computational purity/ploidy estimate fits sequencing copy-number and allele-fraction data. Fitting those existing data uses no additional tissue. Report purity as a fraction or percentage and ploidy as average cancer-genome copies, such as 2.1 or 3.8, with the region, method and model assumptions.

Laboratories set minimum tumour content for the particular assay. Too few tumour cells, contamination, subclonal copy changes or several similarly good model fits can make the estimate uncertain. Purity and ploidy do not identify which mutations drive the cancer or which treatment will work.

records.name: Spatial transcriptomics
records.tldr: These methods measure RNA signals while keeping information about position in a tissue section. A measured spot, an estimated cell boundary and an imputed value are different kinds of evidence.
records.summary: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

Measures and how: RNA with coordinates, by preparing a section, capturing or probing RNA, sequencing or imaging, decoding, registering positions and reporting the assignment rules. Input and tissue cost: protocol-compatible frozen or fixed sections; sectioning and molecular preparation consume allocated material, some workflows alter or destroy the assayed section, and re-scoring existing data consumes no new tissue. Output and units: gene counts per spot, bin or assigned cell, and decoded molecule coordinates, often in micrometres, with physical dimensions, normalisation and observed-versus-imputed labels kept. Thresholds: assay-specific gene or probe coverage, capture and decoding quality, background and segmentation criteria; no universal high-expression or neighbourhood cutoff. Failure modes: poor RNA, incomplete probe coverage, low capture, image-registration errors, inaccurate segmentation, spillover and unsuitable reference models. Limits: no automatic single-cell identity, complete transcriptome, whole-tumour representation, proven interaction or clinical selection rule. Validation tier: many workflows are research methods, so check analytical and intended-use validation for the exact assay and model; resolution claims and regulatory status are separate questions.

Figure reading (fictional geometry, no platform scale): a capture spot is one barcode that can pool several cells. Imaging decodes six RNA coordinates, three for gene G and three for gene H (3 + 3 = 6), and these are coordinates, not cell labels. Moving the estimated cell masks changes which cell a coordinate is assigned to while the RNA stays fixed. Gene R is absent from the G and H panel, so a model-inferred R value is not an observed molecule, and RNA position is not protein or function.

In a fictional map, each of two regions contains twelve illustrative immune cells, but one places them within malignant nests and the other outside. Equal cell symbols do not guarantee equal bulk RNA: similar RNA is a separately stipulated condition of the example. The map supplies neither a stromal-area TIL score nor evidence of recognition or treatment benefit. A capture spot can pool several cells, and changing an estimated cell boundary can change molecule assignment while the observed RNA coordinates stay fixed. Each region also has six malignant symbols; eight immune-cell centres fall inside the first nest contour and none inside the second. The contour is a regional boundary, not a cell membrane or a measured transport barrier.

records.name: Spatial proximity metrics
records.tldr: These measurements describe where different cells sit in a tissue section. Distance, density and mixing answer different questions and do not by themselves show interaction or predict treatment benefit.
records.summary:
Spatial proximity analysis describes relationships between typed cells at specified positions in sampled tissue. Radius counts, nearest-neighbour distances, G-cross curves, mixing scores and cellular neighbourhoods answer different questions. Their definitions depend on cell calls, region selection, reference populations and physical distance rules.

A map can support a biological hypothesis or a cohort association while leaving functional interaction and clinical usefulness unresolved. Read the exact assay and sampling design, preserve the denominator and validate the same measurement before extending a result to another setting.

notes: A spatial proximity analysis begins with a sampled section, estimated cell types and positions. Staining, imaging, cell segmentation and typing create that list; errors in boundaries, marker assignment or signal spillover can therefore create false neighbours. Density asks how many cells occupy a stated area, while proximity asks how one cell type is positioned relative to another. Keeping the analysis box and its tissue compartments visible is as important as reporting the final number.

A compartment density might be CD8 T cells per square millimetre of tumour epithelium or stroma. A radius count can ask how many cells of type A lie within a chosen distance of a type B cell; a population fraction also states which cells form its denominator. A nearest-neighbour analysis measures, for each cell of type A, the distance to the closest cell of type B and may summarise those distances by their median. Define whether distances use cell centres or boundaries; the same pair can have different values under these rules.

The directed G-cross function gives the fraction of reference cells of one type whose nearest cell of the other type lies within each radius. It is a curve over distance. Its value at 20 micrometres and its area from zero to 20 micrometres are different summaries. The fixed-radius fraction is unitless; an unnormalised area over distance has distance units, so report any normalisation. A curve, a map of local values and a clustered neighbourhood assignment also need not reduce to one number per slide. Name the actual output and aggregation rule.

Mixing scores have method-specific definitions. Keren's score divided immune-tumour neighbour interactions by immune-immune interactions in an image-derived neighbour matrix. Maley's Morisita-Horn approach instead assessed spatial overlap in the distribution of immune and cancer cells on histology images. These are not interchangeable measurements. Cellular-neighbourhood analysis groups recurring local cell-type compositions: Schürch's 2020 method used a ten-cell nearest-neighbour window including the centre cell, rather than ten additional cells, and clustered those compositions.

One micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre, so 20 micrometres is 0.020 millimetres. A distance threshold is not evidence of membrane contact. In a fictional geometry with equal circular cells seven to ten micrometres wide, centres 20 micrometres apart leave a gap of ten to 13 micrometres. This calculation does not establish a biological lymphocyte-size range. Cell dimensions, shape and the choice of centres or boundaries must be measured or specified for the actual image.

For a contact-dependent mechanism, immune cells retained in stroma face a different spatial question from cells among cancer cells. Position alone leaves antigen recognition and functional capacity unmeasured: a T cell 15 micrometres from a cancer cell need not be recognising or killing it. A two-dimensional slice also samples only part of a three-dimensional structure. Lin and colleagues' colorectal-cancer study reconstructed interconnected lymphoid networks from apparently separate two-dimensional domains; only one cancer was reconstructed in three dimensions in that study.

Elomaa and colleagues analysed 983 colorectal-cancer patients and an independent validation cohort of 246. Their score combined percentile-ranked CD3 and CD8 tumour-to-T-cell G-cross values at 20 micrometres in the tumour centre and invasive margin. It was not simply an area under a G-cross curve. High versus low score was associated with longer cancer-specific survival: adjusted hazard ratio 0.33, 95% confidence interval 0.20 to 0.52, and 0.15, 0.05 to 0.45, respectively. Its prognostic value was independent of their T-cell density score; these are cohort associations.

Gide and colleagues examined pretreatment metastatic-melanoma specimens from 27 patients receiving anti-PD-1 alone and 34 receiving anti-PD-1 with ipilimumab. Responders had higher densities of CD8 T cells within 20 micrometres of melanoma cells in both groups. This was an association in treated cohorts, rather than a randomised comparison proving that the spatial measurement selects who benefits from adding treatment.

Maley and colleagues assessed immune-cancer colocalisation on routine histology in discovery and validation sets of 486 and 516 breast-cancer samples from women; 475 and 514 had survival data. Colocalisation was associated with disease-specific survival and effects varied by subtype. Walker and colleagues' retrospective study of 1,467 participants defined proximity and consistency from the mean and variance of nearest-neighbour distances between cancer and CD8 T cells. These measures were associated with recurrence-free survival more strongly than lymphocyte counts in the reported analyses. Neither study demonstrates benefit from choosing immunotherapy using its measurement.

In Keren's 41-patient triple-negative breast-cancer cohort, mixed and compartmentalised immune architecture was linked to survival. Their mixing threshold was chosen to reduce within-group and increase between-group variability; it is not a universally validated cutoff. A useful association in one dataset does not establish that a distance or mixing rule was locked and then prospectively validated for treatment selection.

The six-institution MITRE study optimised a specified six-marker PD-1/PD-L1 fluorescence workflow and used a locked image-analysis algorithm. It counted neighbouring PD-1-positive and PD-L1-positive cells within 25 micrometres, rather than measuring receptor binding. Reported average intersite R-squared was 0.82 for the breast-cancer tissue microarray and 0.84 for the lung-cancer microarray. R-squared describes a linear-fit relationship in these measurement comparisons, not 82% accuracy in predicting patient benefit. Reproducibility of this defined workflow is separate from clinical prediction or utility.

Stromal tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte scoring estimates the proportion of stromal area occupied by lymphocytes on a histology section. It is compartment-based assessment rather than a T-cell-to-cancer-cell distance. Page and colleagues' 2023 working-group report describes its standardisation and evaluation across datasets alongside the distinct colon-cancer Immunoscore. That evidence does not automatically validate a new proximity assay, and it does not rank every existing or future spatial method.

In a fictional region containing 200 CD8 T cells, 60 within 20 micrometres of a cancer cell is 30% of the CD8 cells. Moving the box two millimetres into stroma can give 15 near cancer among 300 CD8 cells, or 5%, with the same tumour, stain and radius. The counts are invented to demonstrate region dependence. They do not establish a biological difference caused by treatment or a patient cutoff.

Specify direction as well as radius. The share of CD8 T cells with a cancer-cell neighbour uses CD8 cells as its denominator; the share of cancer cells with a CD8 neighbour uses cancer cells instead. These can differ even on the same map. Similarly, thresholds of ten, 20 and 30 micrometres define different measurements; a result under one definition cannot be transferred to another without checking it.

A measurement report identifies the section and whether it came from a biopsy or resection, the markers defining each cell type, and how segmentation and cell calls were checked. It states whether the analysis used an entire imaged area or selected regions, who selected them and the rule used. A single section, its chosen regions and multiple fields from one specimen are not interchangeable samples of the whole tumour.

Report the cell-type pair, the reference population, the distance definition, the radius and any aggregation or normalisation. State whether a cutoff was fixed before looking at outcomes or chosen to fit this cohort, and whether the same definition was evaluated in an independent group. Analytical reproducibility, prognostic association, differential treatment benefit, prospective validation of a locked rule and regulatory approval are separate claims. The cited cohort studies do not establish an exhaustive statement about all approved spatial tests.

If a fictional report says cells became 3.2 times closer after treatment, first establish which distance or score was compared. Check region-selection rules in both samples, comparable specimen types, the same fixed metric and radius, and variation between sections of the same block. The ratio alone does not establish a change in immune recognition, interaction or patient outcome.

records.name: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs)
records.tldr: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes are lymphocytes found in tumour tissue. Their identity, location, measurement denominator and function answer different questions.
records.summary: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are lymphocytes found in sampled tumour tissue, including T- and B-cell populations. The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by a defined mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within eligible tumour-associated stroma on H&E sections. Higher pretreatment scores were associated with better outcomes in the cited early triple-negative breast cancer cohorts, but those associations do not guarantee an individual outcome or establish extra benefit from pembrolizumab. Intratumoral location, stromal area, immune-cell counts and cells expanded for TIL therapy are different measurements or uses.

notes: The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by mononuclear inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and plasma cells, as a percentage of eligible tumour-associated stroma. It is not the percentage of all cells, a CD8-cell count or the fraction of cancer cells being killed.

Define the eligible region and treatment setting before estimating the percentage. Use the specified exclusions for normal structures, in-situ disease, necrosis, crush damage and biopsy-site changes, and assess the region overall rather than only its hottest spot. A prognostic association does not establish added benefit from a particular treatment.

In the pooled analysis of 2,148 early-stage TNBC patients given anthracycline-based chemotherapy with or without taxanes, each 10 percentage-point increase in pretreatment stromal TILs corresponded to an adjusted invasive disease-free survival hazard ratio of 0.87 (95% confidence interval 0.83 to 0.91) and overall survival hazard ratio of 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89). These associations do not establish an added pembrolizumab benefit by TIL level.

Among 906 TNBC patients from six neoadjuvant chemotherapy trials, pathological complete response occurred in 80 of 260 with low TILs (0% to 10%), 117 of 373 with intermediate TILs (11% to 59%) and 136 of 273 with high TILs (at least 60%): about 31%, 31% and 50%. These categories describe that analysis and are not universal treatment cutoffs.

Fictional area exercise: region A has 4 units of eligible stroma with 0.4 occupied by infiltrate; region B has 1 unit with 0.6 occupied. Pooled occupied area is (0.4 + 0.6)/(4 + 1) = 20%. Averaging the regional percentages without area weighting gives (10% + 60%)/2 = 35%. This arithmetic illustrates the denominator; it does not prescribe a pixel workflow for clinical semiquantitative scoring.

A fictional sTIL estimate of 30% means that the defined mononuclear infiltrate occupies about 30% of eligible stromal area. It does not mean 30% of all cells are lymphocytes or CD8 cells, or that 30% of cancer cells are being killed. Intratumoral TILs, positive-nucleus fractions, cells per square millimetre and bulk immune RNA measure different things. Additional stains change the measurement rather than silently changing its denominator.

Residual-disease recommendations assess the residual tumour bed rather than simply reusing untreated invasive borders. Keep specimen type, site, treatment setting and observer calibration. A high score does not prove tumour-specific recognition, entry into every malignant nest or a permanent hot-tumour state.

To interpret a stromal TIL estimate, retain the block, sampled site, specimen type and treatment setting, then define the eligible stromal region and its exclusions. The output is a continuous estimated percentage of that area occupied by the specified infiltrate. State whether a trained observer or a computational method produced it, with calibration and regional sampling where relevant. Artifacts, sparse stroma, heterogeneity, observer variation and an unrepresentative sample can limit the result. The section uses finite tissue, and measurement reproducibility is a separate question from validation for clinical treatment selection.

TIL is a location label, CD8 is a phenotype and antigen specificity is another property. Simoni found bystander CD8 cells recognizing viral rather than cancer epitopes in human lung and colorectal tumours; the study’s CD39 associations are not a universal test of every cell’s target. A functional assay compares defined effectors and targets with recognition and target-survival controls. Neither presence, cytokine release nor one killing assay reproduces every access barrier or establishes clinical benefit.

The Loi analysis pooled nine studies. In its node-negative subgroup with at least 30% stromal TILs, three-year overall survival was 99% (95% CI 97% to 100%) after the specified adjuvant chemotherapy. Denkert’s pooled neoadjuvant population contained 3,771 patients overall, including the 906 TNBC patients described above. These population and subgroup findings do not make the study categories universal beneficial-TIL thresholds or establish additional pembrolizumab benefit by score.

In a fictional section, 0.4 square millimetres of mononuclear infiltrate within 2 square millimetres of eligible stroma gives 20% by area. Separately, 30 CD8 cells among 100 counted lymphocytes gives 30% of those counted lymphocytes. Neither is the fraction of all tumour cells, a measure of cancer specificity or evidence of useful killing. One occupied unit among five equal eligible stromal-area units also gives 20%; the drawing illustrates a denominator rather than prescribing pixel counting for semiquantitative breast scoring.

Fixed sections and morphology or selected stains can measure identity, compartment and abundance; viable-cell assays ask about phenotype and function. Dissociation loses native location, culture can select populations and tests consume finite material. Keep cells per square millimetre, specified cell fractions, stromal-area percentages and assay-specific function distinct. TIL therapy is a manufactured expanded-cell product: a tissue count does not establish product yield, composition, potency or treatment success. Sampling, damage, mixed compartments, unsuitable markers and culture selection are different failure modes, and descriptive pathology, research function and clinical treatment selection require different validation.

records.tldr: Tumour-bed cellularity estimates cancer-occupied area within a defined treated breast bed. The in situ share uses a different denominator.
records.summary: Label the region, numerator and denominator before interpreting cellularity. Overall cancer area and the in situ share of that cancer are separate RCB inputs, neither interchangeable with sequencing purity or a score by itself.

notes: For RCB, overall cancer cellularity estimates the area occupied by invasive plus in situ cancer within a defined residual breast bed. The in situ percentage instead uses the cancer component as denominator. Microscopic review can revise bed boundaries and should represent sparse as well as dense regions; selecting only a dense focus changes the measurement.

Invasive bed fraction equals overall cancer fraction multiplied by one minus the in situ fraction of cancer. In a fictional 100-unit bed with 20 units of cancer, 25% in situ means 5 bed units in situ and 15 invasive. The invasive share is 75% of cancer but only 15% of the whole bed. These idealised area units teach denominators, not counting instructions or the precision of a clinical estimate.

Area occupied by cancer, the proportion of counted cells that are malignant and the fraction of sequenced DNA contributed by cancer have different denominators. A selected assay block may also differ from the whole residual bed. Do not enter an area-cellularity estimate as sequencing purity or describe 25% of cancer as 25% of the bed.

Retain the named bed, specimen, treatment setting, mapping and representative sections, overall area percentage and in situ share separately. Incomplete sampling, a misdefined bed and heterogeneous distribution can bias the estimate; staining or sampling consumes finite tissue. There is no universal low/high cellularity cutoff that alone selects treatment.

Cellularity alone supplies neither nodal burden, final margins, distant status, pCR nor an RCB score. CAP's residual-invasive RCB span excludes DCIS, while the MD Anderson protocol estimates invasive plus in situ area in a microscopically revised cancer bed. Neither is interchangeable with the largest contiguous ypT focus. CAP advises against RCB score/class after neoadjuvant endocrine therapy, although individual residual measurements may still be useful.

The MD Anderson protocol estimates overall cellularity and in situ percentage to the nearest 10%, with additional 1% and 5% choices for low values. The 25% in situ example above is fictional denominator arithmetic outside those listed estimation increments. Its arithmetic remains 20 × 0.25 = 5 in situ and 20 - 5 = 15 invasive bed units. A separate protocol-aligned 20% in situ illustration would give 4 in situ and 16 invasive units. Neither should be confused with the RCB example using 50% in situ.

Two fictional treated breast beds can have the same dimensions while one contains sparse residual carcinoma and the other dense residual carcinoma. The footprint alone cannot distinguish their viable cancer area. Read overall cancer area and the in situ share of that cancer with their different denominators, then keep regional nodes and final margins separate. A DCIS-permitting breast-and-node pCR definition can be met when DCIS remains at an involved final edge but no residual invasive breast or nodal cancer is found. Add an involved regional node and that combined endpoint is no longer met, even with a negative blood assay; this does not by itself establish distant spread.

records.name: KEAP1
records.tldr: KEAP1 helps a protein-tagging complex control the NRF2 stress response. A KEAP1 variant, an NRF2 output and a cancer cell’s dependence on that response are separate findings.
records.summary:
NFE2L2 encodes NRF2, a transcription factor; KEAP1 is an adaptor linking it to a CUL3-containing ubiquitin-ligase complex. Under suitable unstressed conditions, tagging promotes NRF2 degradation. Reduced turnover can make more NRF2 available for nuclear stress-defense programs. Protein turnover, nuclear output, protection against a stressor and survival dependence require separate measurements.

Zhang's biochemical and cell experiments found stress-associated inhibition of NRF2 ubiquitination without disruption of every KEAP1-NRF2 association. The lesson's paired conditions depict altered turnover, not creation of NRF2 or a mandatory physical latch release. CUL3 is a scaffold used with other adaptors and substrates, so a CUL3 change cannot be assigned an NRF2 effect from its name alone.

In a fictional culture, high NQO1 RNA, nuclear NRF2, several responsive proteins and reduced readouts after controlled KEAP1 restoration support a regulatory consequence. Test survival under a defined stress separately, using a specific NRF2 perturbation, matched controls and appropriate restoration to assess dependence. Stronger defenses may confer resistance; their abundance does not demonstrate ferroptosis sensitivity or benefit from an NRF2-directed therapy.

Singh sequenced 54 non-small-cell lung tumors and found KEAP1 mutations in ten, about 19%, alongside a separate 12-cell-line analysis. This cohort proportion is not a universal lung-cancer prevalence. Vartanian's proteomic study in A549 and other cell experiments found that brusatol broadly inhibited protein synthesis, so lower NRF2 after that compound does not establish selective engagement. Use cell identity, preservation, timing, several outputs and general-translation controls; no universal NRF2-high treatment cutoff follows.

records.name: HLA (human leukocyte antigen) and MHC
records.tldr: HLA molecules sit on cells and hold up small pieces of the cell's proteins for T cells to inspect. A T cell reads the fragment together with the particular HLA version holding it.
records.summary:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. Kaur and colleagues compared HLA-C*05:01 and HLA-C*07:02 in transfected cells and found differences in expression and recovered peptide breadth. In four B lymphoblastoid cell lines, Schellens and colleagues recovered a small HLA-C-assigned peptide fraction; their assignment procedure gave HLA-A/B precedence because HLA-C prediction was less reliable, and they explicitly expected to underestimate HLA-C. A smaller observed share is therefore not a universal biological fraction or evidence of more permissive binding.

Groove geometry helps explain common peptide lengths without imposing a hard upper limit. Wieczorek and colleagues' 2017 review describes the class-I groove as closed at both ends, usually holding 8 to 10 residues, and the open class-II groove as usually holding 13 to 25. It also describes longer class-I ligands, including solved HLA-A2 complexes with 15-residue peptides. A reported range around 11 is therefore not a ceiling for every class-I ligand. CD4 help does not demonstrate the same target's class-I display. Some CD4 cells can themselves be cytotoxic: Cachot and colleagues directly tested tumour-specific human CD4 cells against tumour cells in defined assays. That result does not make every CD4 response cytotoxic or establish a treatment benefit.

records.name: T-cell receptor
records.tldr: A conventional T-cell receptor recognises a peptide together with its HLA display. Recognition alone does not show killing.
records.summary:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.
